The Root Manual of Noble Mañjuśrī. (Third Part.
Now begins the fiftieth chapter.
Then indeed, the Blessed One Vajrapāṇi, the yakṣa general, was present in that assembly.
Having sat down, he rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and, extending his joined palms toward the Blessed One, bowed in reverence.

He said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, as for that wrathful king named Yamāntaka who was spoken of by Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, its ritual manual (*kalpa*) has not been revealed in detail by the Blessed One, nor by Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta. Blessed One, it is I who, having regard for future generations, [shall explain it] by the Blessed One..."

When the Tathāgata has entered final nirvāṇa and the time for the disappearance of the teaching has arrived, during the period of great terror in this lowest of ages— a buddha-field devoid of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas— for the sake of protecting the teaching of the Tathāgata,
for the sake of ensuring the long endurance of the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), and for the sake of warding off all wicked kings.

O Blessed One, in the final age, in the final time of the Sugata, for the sake of subduing those who harm the Three Jewels, for the sake of fulfilling the inconceivable conduct of a bodhisattva through skill in training sentient beings, and for the sake of accomplishing the inconceivable ripening of sentient beings.

When the destruction of the teaching is occurring, whoever shall employ this King of Wrath named Yamāntaka according to the ritual procedure prescribed in the *kalpa*, for him there will be success. And it will certainly [bring about the subjugation] of wicked kings and of those beings who harm the teaching, as well as great yakṣas of great prowess.
This King of Wrath should be employed against those who are engaged in acts of punishment and favor but are devoid of great compassion, and not against others.
Then the Blessed One entered the meditative absorption called the "Empowerment of Silent Miraculous Transformation. Mañjuśrī remained in silence, and within that circle of the assembly,
six [types of beings] were born.
(Not clear, PDF 16, p.
They attain accomplishment through this mantra as it has been spoken;
wandering over the entire earth, they assume various guises.
Abiding in the realms of various destinies and wombs, they take the forms of dogs and crows;
likewise, they become cats, owls, mice, frogs, and scorpions.
Crowded with all kinds of origins, bodiless yet dwelling within bodies,
they wander the entire earth, uttering the cries of all living beings.
When all beings are submissive and the welfare of all creatures arises as something dear,
and mortals always act accordingly, then one should employ those [mantras] for them.
It is not taught to others in the world, for it is honored by the deities;
it should be known as all-encompassing in every respect and the accomplisher of all mantras.
Whatever has been spoken, and whatever other men on earth shall speak—
all that is the expansion of the Kalpa, as declared here by the Mothers of the World.
Having been addressed in this way, the gods, together with the Sūtrāntas as the fifth,
remained silent and stood there, bowing down to the Bull among Jinas.
He sat down to hear the Dharma in that most excellent assembly,
[together with] the empowerments of all the Buddhas and the sons of the Victors without exception.
Having requested the Great Hero, they remained silent thereafter;
then the glorious Vajradhṛk worshipped the deities.
The hosts of gods were terrified, and all the lords of the world were struck with fear. (Āryamañjuśrī, p. 548)
And all the gods, the nāgas, and the lords of the dānavas, together with their mothers.
All the hosts of gods, led by the chief planets, trembled;
humans trembled with divided minds, and the Pūtanās were filled with evil intent.
Then those kings, distressed and terrified, with hearts full of wrath,
sought refuge in the command of the King of Dharma.
They are terrified of the Lord of the Guhyakas, the Yakṣa Vajrapāṇi of great splendor,
and of Mañjughoṣa, the Prince who is the King of Mantras.
And then he made a solemn pledge in the presence of Mañjughoṣa:
"O Child! O Compassionate One toward all beings! Please protect us!"
Today we shall consume you with cruel and most dreadful mantras;
for today, overcome by anger, we have established ourselves upon the surface of the earth.
Then the Bodhisattva, possessing great splendor, indeed appearing in the form of a child, said:
"Do not fear, O all you gods, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and dānavas!"
Indeed, this vow has been declared by me as one that cannot be transgressed by all the deities,
nor by humans or non-humans, nor by any beings whatsoever.
Always possessing a mind of loving-kindness, one should constantly recollect that mantra—
the Fully Enlightened One, the foremost among bipeds, the Lion of the Śākyas, the supreme among men.
By him alone was the mantra spoken, beginning with Uṣṇīṣa and including Locanā;
it belongs to the Teacher of the Three Worlds, the Wheel-Bearer, the Mass of Splendor, the Source of Victory.
Vijayoṣṇīṣa and the other mantras, Padmapāṇi together with Lokita,
the Lord Avalokita, Bhṛkuṭī, Tārā, and Yaśasvinī.
And the goddess Mahāśvetā Yaśovatī dressed in white garments,
as well as the Vidyā Bhogavatī, and Hayagrīva, the king of mantras.
These mantras in the Mantra-kula are the principal ones, not issued from [any other source];
they are the sole protector, the mantra that brings about the state of the Lord.
Having recollected the God of gods, the Lord of Mantras, of great splendor,
there arose from him the Wrathful One known by the name Yamāntaka.
The thoughts of Avalokiteśvara, which give rise to compassion,
were revealed by the Buddhas of the past— those whose minds are drawn forth by great compassion.
That Tārā, spoken by Avalokita, delivers sentient beings;
she is the noble vidyā born of samādhi, designated as "woman," yet possessing the nature of pure consciousness.
Then the bodhisattva practices the supreme conduct of awakening throughout thousands of world-systems, indeed many times over, innumerable ways.
Then the Goddess, wandering for the sake of the welfare of sentient beings,
assumed the form of a woman through the nature of mantra for embodied beings.
One should establish those beings who are to be disciplined by means of ritual rules in the vehicle of awakening;
thus has the inconceivable conduct of the bodhisattvas been revealed.
One should recollect Vajrapāṇi, the hero likewise, the sovereign of mantras;
and the goddess Māmakī, the mistress of the family, who is honored throughout the three worlds.
Śaṅkulā, Mekhalā, the illustrious Vajramuṣṭi,
Krodhendratilaka, Śatru, Nīladaṇḍa, and Bhairava.
These hosts of female messengers are proclaimed as wrathful ones and presiding deities of the vidyās;
they are all preeminent within the Vajra family, for they are indeed protected by us.
Likewise, Gajagandha, the Bodhisattva of great supernatural power in the world;
and Mahāsthānaprāpta, the wise Bodhisattva of great supernatural power.
If one should then remember Samantabhadra, the most excellent and beautiful eldest son,
no fear shall exist for them at that time.
As well as Māṇibhadra and the supreme Yakṣa Jambhala, who are ever-present—
how could there be any fear for all the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas?
Through the recollection and worship of them, great protection is proclaimed;
then, O gods, there is a vast fruit, which is meritorious and beyond conceptualization.
To the goddess who assumes a female form, who is free from passion and possesses great supernatural power, and who is truly devoted to the Three Jewels and the teaching of the Jina; (pdf 5, p. 550)
When they no longer have any fear regarding friend or foe,
that is said to be the "pledge" (samaya) there, which must not be transgressed by any practitioners.
This is proclaimed as the supreme wrathful [deity] Yamāntaka;
when beings abide in his commitment (*samaya*), all humans shall not eat them.
Then all those gods and non-human beings, with joyful minds,
remained steadfast in their commitment at that time, following the wisdom of the Son of the Jina.
Then the Yakṣa general, enraged at those words of defeat,
caused all the innumerable world-systems to tremble.
Why was this King of Wrath revealed by the Sons of the Conquerors in the past? It was for the purpose of disciplining sentient beings, yet it appears to be without purpose.
The power of the King of Wrath and his ancient emergence were proclaimed;
having been addressed thus, the Wielder of the Vajra then stood firm, having cast down his vajra.
Then the wise youth Mañjughoṣa, possessing great supernatural power and appearing in the form of a child, laughed and uttered these words.
Do not be corrupted, O Great Yakṣa! Vajrapāṇi of great supernatural power!
For this King of Wrath of great supernatural power has indeed been revealed by me.
I shall give you the mantra itself; reveal it as you desire.
It was not possible for you to fully describe the power of Krodha.
For he is seen here, situated within this very body;
indeed, by him you have been drawn, if you ask me about your heart.
For it is not possible to turn back one who is possessed by anger here, O Lord;
indeed, you have revealed this as it truly is, and you yourself have authorized it.
(From *pdf* 6, p. 551):
Abandoned by all the best of mantras among those who have turned away from the teaching, mortals become full of doubt regarding those who lack faith and are situated in suffering.
Those who reject the Sangha of the jewel of the True Dharma should be shunned when one is composed;
likewise those who are naked, always impure with leftovers, and whose conduct and sphere of activity are unclean.

Indeed, [one should not void urine] in an unprotected place, nor in one devoid of mantras, nor where there is constant impurity, nor in a pitiless spot; nor in the dwellings of the gods, at shrines, or in the courtyards and circles of monasteries.
There, those who delight in sexual intercourse will be destroyed by anger;
they have fallen from their commitments, yet they remain complacent, ignorant of the application of mantras.
Their anger may strike down those whose conduct and gait have become faltering;
in the world of all human beings, heedfulness is not found.
Those who are devoted to negligence and do not sever the flaws arising from the violation of their commitments are slain by the King of Wrath, even though they employ the mantras.
In every way, all fools are subject to negligence,
with the exception of those free from passion— the Pratyekabuddhas, Arhats, and Śrāvakas.
"All indeed are to be slain and punished in every way by the King of Wrath," thus was it said by Mañjuśrī with a mind possessed of compassion.
"The conduct of the Buddhas and the great miraculous powers of the Bodhisattvas are inconceivable.
Having spoken thus, they all then remained silent.
Then the glorious Vajradhara again grasped the vajra;
having taken up the vajra, he was pleased and, having attained what had not been sown before, spoke thus.

Thus concludes the forty-eighth chapter, the detailed exposition on the rules, the greatness of the mantras, and the description of the Wrathful King Yamāntaka, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra belonging to the Bodhisattvapiṭaka-avaṃsaka.
(PDF 7, p.
552) Now begins the fifty-first detailed chapter.
Then, Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of the Guhyakas, having surveyed the entire great assembly circle, said:
He addressed all those hosts of beings seated above the Pure Abodes: "Listen, noble sirs,
to [the power] of Yamāntaka, the King of Wrath, who possesses immeasurable strength and prowess,
the tamer of the unsubdued, the ender of Vaivasvata’s life, and who is intent upon the subjugation of wicked beings."
Regarding the Great Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī’s discourse, first of all, there is the procedure for the cloth-painting (paṭavidhāna) of the Great Bodhisattva.
Neither a specific lunar day nor an astrological mansion is prescribed, nor is fasting enjoined;
when fear of enemies has arisen, one should have this painting executed.
Having taken hold of a corpse on the fourteenth or eighth lunar day during the dark fortnight of the month of Kṛṣṇa, one should obtain the garment of a Brāhmaṇa from that [corpse].
Then, having taken it at night, one should dye it with blood;
thereafter, one should again perform purification with water and cause it to be thoroughly dried.
One should have a fierce, wrathful, and terrifying painter depict [the image] in a cremation ground during the dark fortnight; one should complete it in just three nights.
On the nights of the eighth and fourteenth [lunar days], illuminated by lamps of human fat,
the painter always remains there, facing the south.

Having performed the protection rites and being composed, the mantra-practitioner— afflicted by the suffering and fear of enemies— should either draw [the diagram] himself while seated upon a skull-cup.
When the first watch of the night has begun, even an enemy experiences great fear;
when the second has begun, the enemy is overwhelmed by a high fever and falls into a swoon.
If he releases his life-breaths during the third [segment], he will have gone to the next world;
how could there be peace for him when the mantra-practitioner is not pleased?
The body of the enemy indeed withers away, and the destruction of his planetary influence occurs;
by thus painting the cloth, [this happens] at the end of the summer season during a great danger.
Enraged, he was clad in a tiger skin.
(His form) bears various terrible weapons, holds a staff in his hand, and is fearsome;
he has blood-red eyes, is full of wrath, and is marked by the movement of the three-eyed one.
With hair standing erect and matted, smoke-colored in some places and resembling black collyrium in others,
he was terrible, with a luster like an autumnal cloud.
One should depict him resembling the form of Kṛtānta (the God of Death), mounted upon a buffalo,
performing cruel deeds, most terrifying, fierce, and the slayer of Rudra.
Indeed, it destroys twin life, rises up as a slayer of beings, is cruel,
exceedingly violent in all its actions, and is terrifying, calamitous, and dreadful.
Having painted this supreme wrathful one— the terror even of fear, the destroyer of all embodied beings— with pigments made from one's own blood.
One should draw the mixed [designs] with brilliant substances mixed with great animal fat and cow's ghee,
using skull-bowls produced from human bones as well.
Having drawn [the design] with brushes made from the hair of a corpse,
either fasting himself or having it painted by an artist;
It was adorned with abundant offerings of food, flowers, and the like; with red garlands and excellent sandalwood; and with incense made of human flesh and fat, as well as lamps fed by fat.
One should have the excellent cloth-painting made; first, at the end, and in the middle, there is worship.
Having made the cloth-painting clearly distinct, one should give wealth to the artisan.
One should provide a generous price, or whatever else might always satisfy him; one must ensure that he is not harmed, and that his practice of Dharma remains free from fear.
One should perform his work according to his desire; in brief, this is the price for a hero.
The artisan’s labor must be fruitful, and one should avoid that which is devoid of reward.
One should employ [the ritual] in such a way that he becomes fully satisfied;
furthermore, great protection must be provided, for otherwise he will surely die.
One who perishes along with his family should protect himself as well;
by one who has recited the vidyā, this procedure for them is prescribed.
Having made a clearly manifest cloth-painting (*paṭa*) or having beheld one desired by the mind,
one should perform all rites, even those that are fierce and destructive to enemies.
Taking the excellent cloth, one should go wherever desired or wherever wished,
[to encounter] great yakṣas, great kings, and those who are proud of their vast wealth.
[It is not for those] who possess great pride and arrogance, who are cruel and performers of cruel deeds,
who cause harm to the Three Jewels, who are nihilistic, and who are devoid of mantra.
But for those who do not worship the mantras, those who revile their devotees,
and those who revile the practitioners of recitation— of these there shall be utter defeat.
Their application should be performed through rites prescribed by rule against those who are most unrighteous, ever-wicked, and who cause suffering to all living beings.
One should employ against them a rite that instantly obstructs life,
using the leaves, bark, and even the roots of the *ariṣṭa* tree as prescribed.
Fermented gruel mixed with sour substances, powdered human bone,
pungent oil, poison, amlavetasa, and fresh ginger.
Having taken mustard seeds and blood originating from a human being,
and having combined them all together, one should place the cloth in a secluded spot.
Facing south, while the cloth [image] faces north,
one should prepare a fire-pit as desired, using white wood produced from pungent trees.
Having kindled it with wood-shavings and being concentrated upon that sacrificial pit,
one should offer all the materials combined according to the rite prescribed for the oblation.
Having again invoked Agni with the mantras of the Wrathful King,
one should bind the trident mudrā for all rites here.
One should offer eight thousand oblations into the fire-pit with wrath;
when the [appropriate] moment arrives, that death of the son shall occur for the first time.
In the second [dream], the assembly members along with their leaders were indeed present;
in the third, there was the death of that very person for whose sake it was performed.
(From PDF 10, p.
555) When the recitation is performed at midnight in the presence of the cloth-painting for the purpose of slaying enemies, it proceeds exactly accordingly.
The destruction of his kingdom shall occur, and there will arise distress within his army;
fire, great winds, and heavy rains shall manifest.
The entire wheel is struck from all sides by the wheel of the enemy;
he is beset by various calamities and overwhelmed by great diseases.
The entire body of that king will surely wither away, there is no doubt;
his whole house will be crowded and filled with non-human beings.
He finds no peace upon his bed nor upon the surface of the earth;
his home is surrounded by Rākṣasas, Pretas, and flesh-eating demons.
Afflicted and deeply distressed by intense sufferings, he fears everywhere;
the great lords and other deities on earth are powerless to protect him.
Brahmā and the other world-protectors, Śakra and the other lords of the thirty-three gods,
all mantras, all deities, and all that arises in the mundane world.
For one who is wicked, arrogant, and angry, his life ends there;
provided that the reciter has uttered [the mantra] at midnight or at midday.
The wrathful Vaivasvata himself is manifested as King Yama;
having placed the cloth upon the ground during the dark fortnight according to one's desire.
Having performed a great worship and offering (*bali*) at a place arising from a cremation ground or a forest—
such as at a solitary tree, a *liṅga*, a mountain, a remote area, or in caves.
One should always undertake one's practice alone and without a companion,
in a great forest, in a secluded place, or in empty temples.
In an empty temple, by a river, or on the shore of the ocean;
in that place, or nearby, or wherever one desires.
One should always have rituals performed within a distance of one yojana;
one should always have these ritual acts performed by a pure person according to this measurement.
(From *pdf* 11, p. 556):
Or else, established in the immeasurable, having gone to the boundless regions, pure, within the domain of inconceivable mantras, [he perceives] the inconceivable range of mantras.

Inconceivable is the power of the mantras of supernatural success; inconceivable is the accomplishment of those who recite them. Inconceivable is the action that is seen, and the fruit as well is inconceivable.
The great-souled Yamāntaka, King of Wrath,
possesses a field of miraculous power consisting of his activity and his magnificent transformations.
An inconceivable accomplishment of those possessing form is seen here upon the earth;
all Bodhisattvas of great supernatural power are unable to protect it.
How much more so, then, the worldly mantras, along with the grahas and those mātṛs,
as well as Īśāna together with Viṣṇu, and Skanda and Purandara?
At that time, those great-souled Bodhisattvas who abide on the ten stages— both the Victors and the sons of the Victors— were also sustained by you.
For even the Pratyekabuddhas, Arhats, those free from passion, and those of great supernatural power were unable to protect the commitment previously made by them.
I shall speak in brief; listen, you who desire the welfare of beings:
no one else is capable of turning back a reciter who is not well-disposed.
How could there be peace for him here while the supreme mantra remains unsatisfied? Only when it becomes gracious in mind or moistened with compassion might this ever happen.
For the practitioner of the great-souled Yamāntaka, the King of Wrath,
he first attains peace, fortitude, or the preservation of life.
Picumanda, pungent oil, sour gruel, and poison as the fifth;
human blood, human flesh, salt, and furthermore, the three pungents.
Black mustard, conch-shell powder, sour vetasa, fresh ginger,
the roots of dhurdhūraka, and tender [shoots]...
The alkali of castor root, safflower,
[the fruit of] *madana*, garlic, and *gṛñjanaka* (pdf 12,
Having combined all of these— the palāśa, śākhoṭaka, and leek, along with liquor and spirits— one should offer them as oblations into the fire in the presence of the cloth-painting.
When eight thousand oblations have been offered, the destruction of enemies occurs along with their very roots;
indeed, one may destroy all Rajika [mustard], whether auspicious or inauspicious, on the Pāripadya [day].
Its eradication from the root occurs for one who offers oblations during the second junction;
when the third junction has arrived, it occurs for the one who offers oblations while reciting mantras.
Famine shall prevail for him, as well as among the people and the merchant guilds; there shall be drought and great pestilence, and the land shall be overrun on all sides by rākṣasas.
Fire, falling rocks, thunderbolts, and lightning—
these shall afflict his kingdom, province, or country, O lord of men.
In his country, there will be various and manifold calamities, such as the onset of fire-related disasters and likewise the arrival of foreign armies.
Various forms arise through the destruction of great fortune;
one should offer a single root of the *dhurdhūraka* plant as an oblation, and madness will befall him.
For one who constantly offers pungent substances into the fire, it is seized by a great burning sensation;
for one who offers excessively sour substances into the fire, a great fever arising from cold occurs.
Residing within his body, it may overcome wicked kings who are arrogant of their power,
as well as cruel great yakṣas, wealthy men, and those supported by vast armies.
His life will last for two nights or seven nights until his death;
one should write down whichever deity he worships or his name according to the lunar mansion (nakṣatra).
Having fashioned an image from the charcoal of a cremation ground and placed it before a cloth painting on the ground,
one should perform the recitation while enraged, starting from the feet up to the head.
Suddenly, O lord of men, that king is seized by various piercing pains;
overcome by a great disease, he dies at that very moment.
Furthermore, animals that are mutilated or deformed, as well as those that are fit for consumption by cruel and depraved beings.
(From PDF 13, p.
558) He is also slain by flesh-eaters, pūtanas, piśācas, pretas, and mātṛs,
as well as by his own servants, due to that very [negligence].
Then the glorious Vajradhara, having spoken thus to the assembly,
paid homage to all the Buddhas and thereafter remained silent and steadfast.
Desiring the welfare of the worlds, he spoke thus once more:
[this] mantra for all the hosts of yakṣas and for all the yakṣiṇīs in every respect.
Then the Bodhisattva Yakṣa General indeed spoke;
he chose a chapter on yakṣīs that was accompanied by all ritual applications.
When a mantra practitioner desires sexual union— whether blinded by passion or of deluded intellect— he performs the summoning of all, the subjugation, and the extraction of all thorns.
It cannot be warded off by remedies or by the commands of the Sugatas,
for it has been practiced since beginningless saṃsāra by those who have long suffered.
The Tathāgatas have declared that their destination is painful and even more painful;
however, one who practices celibacy and has conquered the senses attains a beautiful destination.
Having been taught what is auspicious and propitious, one shall attain peace at the end;
having ascended to the equality of the three vehicles, one shall finally attain perfect nirvāṇa.
Those who are perverted, blinded by passion, and seized by evil destinies— such ascetics wander through the five states of existence within the terrible thicket of saṃsāra.
For the sake of those who are suffering, the enjoyment of sensual pleasures is indeed described;
yet they are liberated from all evil, having turned away from the threefold faults.
"Possessed by the command of the Teacher, they are liberated from all bonds."

The forty-ninth chapter, the second detailed section on the rules for the sorcery of the wrathful king Yamāntaka, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka,
is completed.
(From PDF 14, p.
559) Now follows the fifty-second detailed chapter.
Then, indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Śāntamati was present, having assembled in that very gathering of the assembly.

He sat down. Rising from his seat, he bowed to all the Buddhas and, standing in the midst of the assembly circle, circumambulated the Blessed One Śākyamuni three times, prostrated at his feet, and looking toward Vajrapāṇi, the great yakṣa general, he uttered these words: "You are exceedingly cruel."

O Vajrapāṇi, you who proclaim mantra-tantras that cause harm to sentient beings and are associated with sensual desires— surely, O Son of the Conqueror, this is not the way of the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas! For the great Bodhisattvas practice the conduct of a Bodhisattva as manifested by great compassion.

Though they have set out with the resolute intention for the welfare and benefit of all sentient beings, they are not released from the bonds of existence. Furthermore, O Son of the Victor, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones, being endowed with great compassion, do not preach a Dharma teaching that harms sentient beings for the sake of all beings.
They have set out with the resolute intention to bring benefit to all sentient beings.
Then indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi addressed the Bodhisattva Śāntamati:

"In this very way, Śāntamati, a Bodhisattva should train; in this way should he practice—just as you speak, just as you proclaim. Such is the manner of all Buddhas and of the Bodhisattvas of great supernatural power."
In that same way, I shall explain it according to the ultimate truth.
By relying upon the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), one is liberated at the limit of phenomena (dharmakoṭi);
indeed, the limit of sentient beings is inconceivable, and their ripening is likewise inconceivable.
The qualities of a Buddha are indeed inconceivable, and the conduct leading to enlightenment is inconceivable; for, having regard for the beings to be trained, their conduct is truly inconceivable.
The conduct of the bodhisattvas is proclaimed to be inconceivable;
this tantra among all mantras is likewise inconceivable due to its power.
The sphere of supernatural power and the inconceivable majesty of the movement of the great-souled Yamāntaka, the King of Wrath, are both inconceivable.

O Śāntamati, the accomplishment of the conduct and the manifestation of the realm of reality of the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, is indeed inconceivable. Thus, O noble ones, a Bodhisattva who recites mantras should generate the thought [of awakening] in this way.
(As stated in *pdf* 15, p. 560:

"Granted, for the sake of this being, one might produce much demerit and even undergo rebirth in the great hells; yet this being would certainly not produce a greater mass of demerit. May it not be that this being..."

He would become incapable of attaining the three types of enlightenment. Thus, Śāntamati, a bodhisattva who recites mantras should establish his mind in this way and apply both skillful means and the rite of *abhicāruka*. In all ritual actions, he should be one who perceives the signs (*nimitta*), and not one who perceives what is unwholesome, while taking into account the necessity of training sentient beings.
One should train with a mind permeated by compassion.

Moreover, O Son of the Victor! All the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, realize the non-distinction between dharma and adharma, the auspicious and the inauspicious, the greatness of the states of the wholesome and the unwholesome, the non-distinction of the means for training sentient beings, and the non-distinction of the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu); they likewise realize the skillful means for teaching the Dharma to sentient beings.

They practice accordingly. In the very same way, O sons of the Conqueror, we must train ourselves; that is to say, for the sake of disciplining oneself and for the ripening and instruction of sentient beings. Therefore, O venerable sons of the Conqueror, all of you who are seated here in this great assembly of the maṇḍala should listen with full attention.
One must have faith and must become one who seeks what is wholesome and unwholesome;
that is to say, one must become one who delights in the Dharma-teachings of the Tathāgata.
Then the bodhisattva mahāsattva Śāntamati, having looked toward Vajrapāṇi, the general of the yakṣas,

while gazing upon the Buddha, the Blessed One.

Then Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of Guhyakas, having surveyed that entire assembly circle, spoke again the ritual manual of the Wrathful King: "Listen, O hosts of gods, and all you multitudes of spirits who have issued from the realm of sentient beings! First, having performed the protection, [one should approach] that cloth-painting."

Having taken hold of the King of Wrath (Krodharāja) and gone to a secluded place, in a temple of Maheśvara with a single linga, one should smear that linga with poison, blood, mustard seeds, and sour gruel; worship it with *picumarda* leaves;
fashion a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) for oneself from a string of human intestines; and, holding a human skull-cup in the right hand, strike it.
Brandishing his phallus with the index finger of his left hand, overcome by supreme rage,
his mind filled with indignation toward those wicked kings who had insulted him, [he was surrounded] by rogues,
men of wealth, great tyrants, and powerful leaders, as he [entered] the pure enclosure... [of the fire].

With his topknot loosened, having stepped upon the *liṅga* of Maheśvara with his left foot, he should recite the *krodha-mantra* until the *liṅga* of Maheśvara splits in the middle; [this occurs] when it has split into two parts and a great *huṃkāra* [resounds].

It is heard [in the scriptures]: therefore, one should not be afraid. One should recite the mantra right there for a short while, until at that very instant the life of the enemy comes to its end in death. If...
If one recites it until the end of the night, that entire family perishes.
There is another rite as well: at midday, having gone likewise to a temple of Maheśvara, one should worship with nimba leaves, offer incense of human flesh (*mahāmāṃsa*), and recite the mantra.
[The result is that] the enemy’s house is consumed by fire and the enemy suffers from a great fever and trembling. If one does not perform the recitation...

If one who is angry abandons [the rite] or stands facing Dakṣiṇāmūrti, that enemy shall die and there will be the destruction of his lineage. Now, if one performs the restoration: having again washed the *liṅga* with water, one should bathe it with very cold milk; then again with cow's milk. It becomes restored to health.

There is another rite as well: having kindled a fire with *madanakaṇṭaka* wood at the southern face (*dakṣiṇāmūrtti*) of the Liṅga of Maheśvara, one should offer eight thousand oblations of *vaikaṅkata* fuel-sticks smeared with poison, blood, and black mustard seeds. All enemies [shall be afflicted] with a great disease.

They are seized; they become powerless in all their activities. In all countries, all enemies shall become well-disposed. It destroys all mechanical devices and causes them to fall. In brief, however it is employed—even through the ritual procedures of all mundane and supramundane mantras—it accomplishes all of that. One desires accomplishment; by desiring it with the mind, one causes an enemy to be slain when joined with the Great Trident Mudrā, and performs all rites.

There is another ritual as well: at midday, having stayed for one night in a cremation ground on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should kindle a fire with wood from that cremation ground and [throw] black mustard seeds smeared with poison and blood [into it].

One should offer oblations. Then all the *pretas* arrive, making sounds of "hā hā. One must not be afraid. Then one should say, "Kill my enemy! Having said, "So be it," they disappear. They perform [them].

There is another ritual as well: in a secluded and pure place, having entered an empty house while clothed in clean garments, one should offer eight thousand oblations of cotton seeds (*karpāsāsthi*). Then, taking that ash with both hands, one should bind it separately in two pieces of clean cloth, making two small packets (*poṅgalikā*).

Having placed it in a hollowed-out earthenware bowl and established a great protection for himself and his materials, he should not enter his home but go to a great cremation ground. On the night of the fourteenth or the eighth day of the dark fortnight,

Becoming fearless, one who is enraged should recite the mantra ten thousand times; it becomes perfected (*siddha*). If any non-human being should demand that ash as a substance, it must not be given. If he uses force, one should remember the King of Wrath (*Krodharāja*) and employ the *huṃ* syllable; at that very moment, he perishes. This is the procedure for all obstacles.

One should apply the mark of ashes held in the left and right hands. Having performed protection with vigilance, one should return. At dawn, at sunrise, having bathed, being pure and clothed in clean garments, one should enter one's own home, or go to whatever other place is desired. Then, that which was held in the right hand—

With that ash, one should strike the heads of humans, bipeds, quadrupeds, and all living beings— including gods, nāgas, and yakṣas— and they become submissive. Or, with the ash held in the left hand, one should strike the heads of all humans and non-humans, and of all women, and they become submissive.

With the ashes taken with the right hand, one should strike the navel region of men; they become impotent. One should also powder the private parts [of a man], and he becomes incapable. She becomes incapable of serving another man excessively; she becomes one who attains that very same man as her state of being. Again, for her, that [incapacity] manifests: she is unable to practice the conduct of sexual desire.

Furthermore, there are various specific types of bedding and seating, coverlets and robes,
diverse and excellent ornaments, various garments, as well as all specific requisites such as vehicles, carriages, sandals, and umbrellas;
and all things for the body’s use, such as food, drink, and edibles.

One should sprinkle all the vessels and utensils—those for flowers, betel, fruits, perfumes, incense, and so forth—with those respective ashes. The bodies of the enemies will become completely infested with lice, bedbugs, and worms;
they will be eaten by them, struck by various sufferings, and shall die within seven nights. They will be rendered powerless.
All physicians and all gods are unable to ward it off; all mantras are unable to protect [the person], except for that which has been given by him.

Now, as for the restoration: having combined liquorice (*yaṣṭīmadhu*), blue lotus (*nīlotpala*), and white sandalwood (*śvetacandana*), one should grind them with cold water and smear that [mixture] upon the body, starting from the head down to the soles of the feet, while reciting the mantra. He becomes restored to health.

This is the ritual procedure: having gone to a woman who has been possessed by [spirits], one should apply this at a place where one desires it, against all wicked *ḍākinīs* and those who have been crushed, but not against others. Standing behind her, one should scatter ashes.
Having contemplated with the mind, all the vulvas and breasts are removed; even for a man, the male organ, the beard, and the breasts appear.

In this way, one performs many various and diverse actions, or causes them to be performed by another; or one causes them to be performed by whomever pleasure arises, whether it be a woman or a man; or, wherever satisfaction of the mind arises, having given that person ashes, one causes them to act as desired. And this is by way of application.
One should instruct [the disciple] thus: "In this way, one causes [the affliction] to be seized by great diseases. Having thought it with the mind, by touching the head, a headache arises;

By means of the calves and diseases arising from blood, such as those involving corrupted blood and so forth, he causes [the victim] to be seized by disease. He performs [the rite]: having gone near the hut, he stands with the wind at his back and casts that very ash [into the fire]. Both the rampart held by the hands, the gateway, and the watchtowers collapse. Then a great conflagration breaks out in the superintendent’s residence. Having cast everything aside, he either flees or falls into capture. In this way, he performs various kinds of rites as desired for the destruction of enemies, for his own great protection, or for that of his army or friends. Now, for one desiring to accomplish the practice of a yakṣiṇī:
Naṭī, Naṭa, as well as Bhaṭṭa, and the renowned Revatī; likewise the Asurī Tamasurī, Mekhalā, and Muṣekhalā.

Threatening with her right hand and holding a tree branch with her left hand,

One should offer eight thousand oblations of items anointed with curd, honey, and ghee, three times a day for seven days.

Having assumed her own form, she arrives. Once arrived, she asks, "What must I do? Then the practitioner should say, "Become my wife. Having said, "So be it," she disappears. He becomes a rival to a great yakṣa. If he does not come on the second occasion, one should recite the mantra together with the King of Wrath; then he will certainly come. If he still does not come, [the practitioner] will wither away and die.

The mantra for Naṭṭā is: *oṃ naṭṭe śuklāmbaramālyadhāriṇi maithunapriye svāhā*. The ritual procedure for this is the same as before. The mantra for Bhaṭṭā is: *oṃ bhaṭṭe bhaṭṭe ālokini kiṃ cirāyasi padmehi āgacchāgaccha*.

"Perform my task, svāhā! This [mantra] is accomplished even without a cloth-painting. She becomes a wife who grants all desires. If she enters his home, he lives for five thousand years;
if not, he lives for five hundred years right here, wandering about. He sports with her and accomplishes [his goals].
Together with her, he goes wherever he desires. He bestows upon him an elixir of life (*rasāyana*).
The mantra of Revatī (pdf 21, p. 566): Homage to all yakṣiṇīs! Oṃ, O red one, you who have a red radiance and are anointed with red unguents, svāhā!

The Yakṣī, beautiful in all her limbs, is always devoted to the enjoyment of sensual pleasures;

The mantra of Tamasundarī is: *oṃ ghṛṇu guhyake ghuṇu ghuṇu guḍe ehyehi guhyake svāhā*. There is no ritual service (*upacāra*) for this. Regarding the procedure for her painting (*paṭavidhāna*): first, one who is pure and dressed in clean garments, on the full moon day, having closed the door in a secluded place that is dark and devoid of light, [should practice] the vidyā.
One should recite [the mantra] ten thousand times; thus the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) is accomplished. Thereafter, one should begin the ritual practice (*sādhana*).

Starting from the full moon until the next full moon, within this interval the rite is performed. At night, at the time of going to bed, having ascended the bed in a secluded and hidden place alone, one should close the door.

Having mixed *saṅkucitakarṇikā* and *vānapuṣpa* with pungent oil (*kaṭutaila*), having washed one's hands and feet, and having empowered the right arm one hundred and eight times with mantras, one should sleep in silence. In this manner, day after day until the full moon, she will certainly arrive at midnight. And once she has arrived, she will not...

She should be consulted; she should be desired through silence for [certain] months. When she consults, she should be consulted. From that time forth, she becomes successful. He bestows elixirs and rejuvenators. Placing [the practitioner] upon his back, he carries him even to Mount Sumeru. At night, he causes him to traverse Jambūdvīpa. He causes even an enemy situated a hundred *yojanas* away to be slain. Whatever he is commanded to do, that he performs.

She accomplishes everything, with the sole exception of approaching another man's wife. The yakṣiṇī named Andhāravāsinī possesses great supernatural power;

Madhuyakṣī, Manojñā, and the seventh, Surasundarī—
these are the seven yakṣiṇīs who act for the benefit of sentient beings.
They wander through this world and indeed across the entire earth;
in just a moment, they fly up to the abode of the gods.
In the battle between the gods and the daityas, those of great supernatural power fought;
they were most righteous, filled with compassion, desiring the welfare of beings, and very affectionate.
They wander upon the surface of the earth for the sake of desiring the welfare of sentient beings;
nothing is difficult for them to accomplish, as they are auspicious performers of all activities.

For the sake of the enjoyment of sentient beings, the Bodhisattva has spoken this mantra of Guhyavāsinī: Oṃ guhile guhamati guhavāsi ānaya bhagavati mayāntikaṃ samayamanusmara svāhā. Having kindled a fire with *khadira* wood, [one should offer] *priyaṅgu* flowers...

One should offer eight thousand oblations of [substances] smeared with ghee at the three junctions of the day for one month; thus the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) is accomplished. On a wooden board, a cloth, or a wall, using non-adhesive pigments and new vessels and brushes—at the very beginning, first, during a festival...

Therein, one should have painted a yakṣiṇī named Guhavāsinī, who dwells in a cave, alone, possessing a divine form and adorned with all ornaments; she is clothed in silk garments, wears a silken upper robe, is golden-hued, and has a variegated and beautiful appearance. One should recite [the mantra] ten thousand times. One should say: "Be my mother. Having said this, she vanishes. From that time forward, she performs all duties like a mother.
He provides food and clothing for a retinue of eight hundred; he protects one who is in distress;

She brings a woman even from a hundred *yojanas* away; she causes her to perform everything that is commanded. This ritual is to be performed at night, not by day.

The ritual action is as in the case of Guhavāsinī; and this should be addressed as "O sisters."

The daughter of Vaiśravaṇa, accompanied by a retinue of five hundred, arrives. Having surveyed that entire quarter of the sky, she stands in the atmosphere in her own form. She says, "What must I do? Then the practitioner should say, "One of three boons should be requested."
Whether she is in the state of a mother, a sister, or a wife—if she is one's mother, her mind must not be defiled;

She accomplishes everything by mere thought alone. Day after day, she gives a thousand dīnāras. For one who wanders about this very Jambūdvīpa, she provides for all needs. When she becomes a sister, she brings that woman even from a hundred yojanas away;

One should sleep on a bed strewn with flowers in a secluded place in the dark, accompanied by the Yakṣiṇī Ekākṣarā. Then a non-human female arrives and anoints one's feet; her palms are soft to the touch with divine bliss.
Merely by her touch, a sleep of divine and pleasant contact arises, such that even at sunrise, at the end of the night, [one remains in that state].

She awakens with difficulty; even when awakened, she should think only of that [man]. She must not be desired, nor should she be spoken to with secret counsel. Then, possessing a divine form, appearing like a newlywed bride, surrounded by female attendants, holding a lamp in her hand, she illuminates the world with her own radiance.

At dawn, it disappears. Having left a pearl necklace worth a thousand pieces of gold upon the bed, he departs day after day, leaving it behind. They bring about [destruction] unto death. For these are the supreme secret-keepers; they are to be kept strictly hidden and cannot endure being disclosed to another being. This very same procedure applies to all yakṣiṇīs; they become either accomplished or unaccomplished depending on whether one confesses [one's transgressions]. One should always avoid sexual intercourse with other women and even with one's own wife.
