it is described as fruitful through the greatness of his conduct, and is well-praised by the virtuous.
O King, whoever among us shall hold even a single mantra from this collection of mantras,
his royal prosperity shall bear fruit, as shall his attainment of long life.
Or may I obtain various enjoyments and pleasures from the best of kings;
and may he not be slain by weapons, nor by poisons, whether stationary or mobile.

Furthermore, in this world of mortals, which is defiled and intent on the machinations of others, there are mantras created by those with rival knowledge, as well as the rites for subjugating *vetāḍas*.
For him there is no fear of fire, nor of enemies, spirits, or others;
neither the body of that king nor even that of any living being is destroyed.
Whoever should uphold or recite this supreme and foremost of sūtras,
with their head bowed in reverence when a battle has arisen;
If one should repeatedly pay homage to the Six Syllables,
neither robbers nor those with raised weapons shall strike him down.
One should cause the youth Kumārakārasambhava, mounted on the back of an elephant and well-seated upon a peacock throne, to descend into battle. (pdf 116, p. 661)
Seeing him in the form of a child, adorned with divine ornaments like a celestial youth, all those hostile people and other folk turned back.
Having mounted upon the flagstaffs a golden or silver [image] worshipped with fragrant incense, well-fixed and properly aligned among the flags and banners;
At that time, one should indeed cause the entire battle, crowded with enemies and prepared with various weapons, to descend upon the opponent in the conflict.
Indeed, as soon as they are seen, humans and non-humans alike, as well as kings and even the lords of the gods, either perish or become utterly bewildered on all sides.
There were also accomplished Vidyādharas who relied upon mantras and tantras,
as well as powerful Rākṣasas and the Kaṭapūtana Mothers.
Various kinds of flesh-eaters, as well as yakṣas, kūṣmāṇḍas, and pūtanas,
were unable even to look upon the raised banner once it was firmly established.
To the youth Viśvakarman, who possesses manifold forms and appearances,
the noble Mañjughoṣa, the sovereign lord of the ten stages.
The great king, a Kṣatriya, was a protector of the earth for those dwelling upon it;
he was faithful, free from ill-will and doubt, and devoted to the Dharma.
Having generated the pure state of a Sugata with a mind permeated by compassion,
they indeed proceeded with this rite described here, desiring reconciliation.
For these have been taught in the scriptures by the Victors who have realized the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu),
concerning the ritual procedures, the application of mantras, and the principles of the tantras upon the surface of the earth.
In the past, by countless supreme Victors who were established within the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu),
this treasury of Dharma was indeed taught to human beings upon the earth.
Long ago, while the war between the gods and the asuras was raging,
his city was indeed then left with its armies destroyed by his enemies.
(From PDF 117, p.
662) At that time, when beings were alone and deprived of their chariots upon the surface of the earth,
they then questioned Kāśyapa, that best of sages and supreme among Jinas.
"What should be done? the Lord of Śacī uttered these words:
"I have been defeated by the terrible asuras and have taken refuge here."
Thus addressed, Maghavān, the performer of a hundred sacrifices, then bowed his head at the feet of that best of sages with his crown touching them, O dwellers of heaven.
Indeed, he who was formerly the thousand-eyed Kauśika sat down;
thus addressed, that best of sages, Kāśyapa, became a Brāhmaṇa.
Then the Prince, the source of the universe, uttered speech with a voice like the song of the kalaviṅka bird—
speech that had previously been proclaimed by the best of Jinas.
This great-souled Mañjuśrī is difficult to perceive, yet he is a powerful manifestation of the *lakṣa*;
he is designated as the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and is the teacher of the profound meaning.
O Lord of the Gods, remember that which the Buddha taught to sentient beings: free from conceptual proliferation, formless, devoid of intrinsic nature, and without abode.
Then, having been remembered by them, the one who has realized the truth appeared there at that very moment as the youth Viśvarūpin.
Where the Blessed One stood together with Maghavan, the lord of the gods,
she approached and, having paid homage to the supreme Jina, spoke these words.
Having prostrated before all the supreme Victors and the one of great splendor, Kāśyapa,
he then spoke these mantras after having received the permission of the Sage.
Homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas whose teachings are unimpeded! Oṃ, strike, strike all fears; destroy, annihilate, terrify, crush, cut, pierce, blaze, blaze! Huṃ huṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā!
As soon as this mantra was spoken by the youth Mañjuśrī, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva,
this great earth shook in six ways as far as the ocean’s edge;
and all the Buddhas, Blessed Ones, throughout infinite and boundless realms, [were likewise shaken] as far as the limits of space.
And these mantra-words have been empowered by all the Blessed Buddhas.
(Jaya Śakra, the lord of the gods, free from fear and the bristling of his hair, struck with wonder and amazement,
his eyes wide open, rose from his seat, prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One, and circumambulated him three times.)

Having seen Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta face to face, and having grasped and taken to heart those mantra-words, he mounted his chariot once again and fled toward where those asuras were; all the asuras then set out toward their own city, Pātāla, which is situated at the base of the great ocean.
With his mind shattered and humiliated, his pride and countenance dejected by the terror of the army, and his weapons fallen away,
he beheld that Lord of the Gods blazing like fire; having turned back from the fire, he departed for his own abode.
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, addressed the Trāyastriṃśa deities:

"Do not fear, O worthy ones! Do not fear! By the power of the Buddha, we have conquered the asuras; let us go to our own city. Come, sirs, play, enjoy yourselves, and amuse yourselves each according to your own pleasure."
Having gone to the excellent abode, those gods, with joyful minds, returned once more to their own dwellings.
Then this thought occurred to Śakra, the lord of the gods: "What if I were to fashion that image in the form of a youth and place it at the top of my banner? Then I would have no fear of the asuras."
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, having taken hold of the great jewel-gem named *Mahāmaṇiratnadyotigarbhaprabhodyotana*,

had an image fashioned in the form of a youth; he then raised that banner and firmly established it upon the summit of the palace in the Sudharmā assembly hall of the gods, in the center of the great city of Sudarśana.
Having made it, he established it.

Then those asuras, headed by Prahrāda and Vemacitrin, did not ascend to the netherworld (pātāla), nor did they attack the gods, nor were they able to approach him as he displayed his supernatural powers or as he turned toward the battle.
This continued for many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of years by human calculation; yet there was no fear of the asuras.
It may be so.
Thus has this been proclaimed by the Blessed Buddhas and the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas of old: it possesses immeasurable qualities and benefits, increasing longevity and health;
thus has this detailed expansion of immeasurable qualities and benefits been told from of old as being infinite. [The word] *aparimitaṃ* means that which is immeasurable.

Those who reject this Dharma-discourse, or harbor doubts about it, or speak with a mind possessed by [demons], saying "this is not the word of the Buddha," will be reborn in the Puṇyaprasavana Great Hell or among the animals.

Or they might say: "Neither the mantras nor the medicinal herbs [are true], nor even the extensive greatness, supernatural powers, and transformations of those bodhisattvas; nor indeed was this spoken by the noble ones, but rather by those who indulge in conceptual proliferation.
Thinking thus, they reject, abandon, and disregard it; or they are unable to hear it and consequently depart from that place.
He said, "There will be great demerit for them."
Those men who, with deluded minds, shall indeed reject this supreme Dharma sung by the best of sages and by the wise sons of the Conquerors.
By that [karma], men go to hell, which is elevated and contains animals—
namely Kālasūtra, Sañjīva, Kṣuradhārā, and Gūthamṛttikā.
Then there is the Kuṇapa hell, the Kṣāranadī river, and again the Jvaradhārā;
furthermore, the terrible Asipatravana forest and the Avavaṃhahava hell.
People go to that hell known in the world as Aṭaṭa, for those of evil deeds— those men who are corrupters of dharma.
That terrible place known as Avīci is renowned throughout the world;
it is the abode of evildoers, filled with loathsome iron walls.
Those people who would violate this Dharma are cooked in that [hell],
including all its festive realms down to Avīci, together with their roots.
Having gone to the end of the infinite realms of hell, there is constant suffering for one who rejects this extensive sūtra, the entirety of the Dharma.
They fall into contempt in the world...
[they] go to the hells ending in Avīci, having come under the power of those who were once powerless.
This [work], known as the *Saṃsūtrakalpa*, adorned with mantras and tantras,
takes as its support the various attainments of the accomplished ones— the unobscured limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
The body has the dharma-realm as its object; it is a cultivation without objective support, extensive, preeminent among chapters, conceptual, and vast in its conceptualization.
This root manual, which is not brief but indeed extensive, has been proclaimed; it is well-arranged by Mañjughoṣa and perfectly honored.
It is free from the extremes of eternalism and nihilism, as well as from both [extremes] and other [conceptual] objects;
it is taught through a sequential transition and is exalted as the embodiment of mantra.
One who constantly rejects the wind, the blue sky, and well-cultivated emptiness will then go downwards, to the lowest state.
Then, having fully accomplished awakening through various kinds of merits acquired over incalculable eons, I [attained it] in the most excellent Jina.
The meaning of the mantra-tantras has been spoken, which reveals the state of rebirth and is free from error;
it is indeed the Root Ritual Manual (Mūlakalpa), purifying, auspicious, and the destroyer of evil.
This chapter has been proclaimed in its full detail, beautiful with the conclusion of the Blue Sūtra;
it describes the greatness of the qualities of kings, applied according to time and place.

The true Dharma for the sons of the Victorious One on this earth, as well as for those born as humans— the teaching of the seven sages, which is the seventh [teaching] of the Victor, was proclaimed by the Chief of the World.
The *Bāṣita-kalpavistāra*, which increases glorious prosperity, is complete with its root and is known as the *Visarapaṭala*; it is honored by the mantra-tantras.
For those mortals on earth who reject this supreme, foremost sūtra— the treasury of Dharma empowered by the Victor— shall go to the Avīci hell until the end of time.
Indeed, throughout many great eons it has been thus described;
yet at some time, on some rare occasion, it may occur among mortals.
One born from a Mleccha becomes poor, diseased, and foolish;
in this world, he incurs contempt and may suffer from leprosy.
Foul-smelling, loathsome, deformed, and indeed blind,
he appears on earth with a terrifying form, always hideous and as harsh as a hungry ghost (preta).
He is skillful yet dejected in mind, with deformed nails and likewise loathsome;
he is being devoured by worms and is tormented by ringworm and itching.
Homeless, supremely radiant, and beyond conversation, he is reborn;
yet the one of poor intellect wanders on, returning again and again.
(From *pdf* 121, p.
666) Furthermore, one who rejects the Dharma-treasury of the Victors— which is honored by their relics—
is [subject to] many sufferings and hardships, as well as many friends who are without protection.
The mortal is born in many ways, overwhelmed by grief and suffering;
wherever his course goes, there the one of evil intellect is born again.
"By rejecting this sūtra, one will be reborn here and there.
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, and placed his right knee upon the ground.

Having paid homage with palms joined and eyes wide open and unblinking, and perceiving that all those sons of the gods from the Śuddhāvāsa heaven and many hosts of beings had assembled to hear the Dharma, they addressed the Blessed One Śākyamuni as follows:

"O Blessed One, it is wonderful! To what extent this Dharma-discourse is most excellently spoken! Therefore, O Blessed One, in the future time there will be beings overcome by improper greed, beings whose minds are intensified by the five corruptions (*pañcakaṣāya*), lacking faith, deceitful, harsh, and of immoral conduct; they [will be unable to master] the mantras."

They will have no faith in the greatness of the goal, the worship, the regulations regarding time and place, the mantra-practices, the fire-offerings, the recitations, and the detailed ritual manuals; thinking them to be the word of a non-Buddha, they will reject them. With afflicted minds, they will pass away and experience painful, intense, harsh, and bitter sensations.
And they will be reborn in the great hells. O Blessed One, how should one act toward those suffering beings? For the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are possessed of great compassion.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having touched Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta on the head, addressed him: "Excellent, excellent indeed, Mañjuśrī!
You who have set out for the sake and welfare of all sentient beings; well done, Mañjuśrī! Thus he spoke to you.

You ask the Tathāgata about this matter. Therefore, Mañjuśrī, listen well; attend closely and properly to it. For the sake, benefit, and happiness of all sentient beings, and out of compassion for the world, I shall speak to you for the sake of gods and humans alike.

O Youth! At the time of death, for one who desires to rely upon the supreme form of the *dharmadhātu*—which directs one toward the path to enlightenment and enters into the practice of all mantras—this secret should be recited.

Homage to all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones! Oṃ! O you who possess the form of a youth, source of the universe, come, come! Quickly, quickly! Bhrūṃ bhrūṃ hūṃ hūṃ! O Jina-jit Mañjuśrī, O you of beautiful glory, deliver me from all sufferings! Phaṭ phaṭ! Pacify, pacify! O you who arise from the dead, arise!

"Destroy my evil, svāhā! This, Mañjuśrī, is your supreme heart-mantra (*paramahṛdaya*), which brings about all peace, destroys all evil, releases one from all suffering, and generates long life, health, sovereignty, supreme good fortune, and eloquence."

As soon as these words, which incite all the vidyārājas and sentient beings, had been spoken by the Buddha, the Blessed One Śākyamuni, this great earth— with its mountains, oceans, and the entire collection of the world-receptacle and its inhabitants— trembled in six ways. Furthermore, all the realms of existence— the realms of hungry ghosts, animals, and the world of Yama— and the sufferings of all sentient beings therein were [pacified].

[The obstacles] are pacified. Furthermore, this King of Vidyās, Mañjuśrī, should be brought to mind. At that time, their minds shall not be inclined toward the rejection of the true Dharma, nor will the wicked Māras find an opportunity to enter, and all obstructors and Vināyakas shall depart. And one should generate the thought: "What have I [done]?"
It is impossible to conceive of or reject the inconceivable qualities of awakening belonging to the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones; for the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, will know this.

Thus concludes the fiftieth chapter, the detailed exposition on the benefits, censures, and majestic powers, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
Now begins the fifty-fifth chapter.

If one offers one hundred and eight oblations of white mustard seeds before a cloth painting (*paṭa*) of the noble Mañjuśrī, directed toward a specific person, that person becomes submissive. To subjugate a woman, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations; she will become submissive.

On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should strike the forehead of Noble Mañjuśrī with eight thousand white flowers; the queen will become submissive. Having fashioned a dog-linga from cow-dung that has not fallen to the ground, one should offer seven oblations before it using a trident made of cow-dung, consisting of white mustard seeds smeared with curd, honey, and ghee.

For three days, whoever is the object of this rite shall come under one's control. To subjugate a maiden, one should offer eight thousand *araṅgaṇa* flowers to the noble Mañjuśrī; she will become submissive. Having fashioned an image out of beeswax and placed it upon one’s own thighs, one should recite the mantra eight thousand times; whoever is the object of this rite shall come under one's control.

In front of the cloth painting, one should offer eight hundred white flowers; whoever one desires will come under one's control. Having combined the navel of a conch shell, *rocanā*, and *tagara*, one should grind them together. Having consecrated this with eight thousand recitations, whoever it is given to—whether in food or in drink—that person will come under one's control. For the subjugation of a Brahmin woman, [one should do so] in front of the cloth painting.

One should offer eight thousand oblations of *bilva* flowers; she becomes submissive. With ashes over which the mantra has been recited seven times, whichever woman one sprinkles becomes submissive. Standing before a woman or a man, one should offer eight thousand oblations; he becomes submissive. For the subjugation of a Brahmin woman, [one should perform this] before a painted image (*paṭa*).

One should offer eight thousand oblations of *bilva* flowers; she becomes submissive. With ashes over which the mantra has been recited seven times, whichever woman one sprinkles becomes submissive. Standing before a woman or a man, one should offer eight thousand oblations; he or she becomes submissive. [One should use] a four-finger-length wooden stick...

One who has consecrated [the mantra] eight thousand times can summon anyone; that person will become submissive. One should offer one hundred and eight or eight thousand white flowers. Taking one flower from there and looking at a woman, one should turn it toward her; she will come and become submissive. Subsisting on milk and barley gruel, [one should fashion] a single footprint or an image made of anthill clay.

Having fashioned an image, one should sit before it and recite the mantra until Vāsuki moves; then success is attained. He gives food to oneself and twelve others. He speaks of the past, the future, and the present.
Subsisting on milk and barley gruel, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times; one obtains enjoyments. For one month, subsisting on alms, [one should continue].

On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight, having fasted for one night and performed a great worship before the cloth painting, one should take hold of the feet of the image and recite the mantra until it moves or becomes immovable, at which point one becomes invisible. One becomes the king of all *siddhas*. Food appears according to one's mental wish. One lives for five thousand years. Having descended into the Ganges River...

One should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times. Afterwards, having fashioned a sand-caitya upon that very cloth and having prepared honey and milk as the oblation, one should perform the fire-sacrifice (*homayitavya*). All the *nāgas* will arrive; whatever one commands, they will all do.
Having ascended a mountain peak and installed the cloth, one should offer oblations of incense-sticks smeared with oil.
(From *pdf* 124, p.

669) Yakṣas come; they perform everything that one commands. Having installed the cloth-painting (*paṭa*) in a forest and having placed honey and long pepper together in one place, one should offer oblations eight thousand times. All vidyādharas come.
They become obedient. Having established a caitya containing the *pratītyasamutpāda* formula beneath a single tree, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times.

Upon the completion of the hundred thousand recitations, a goldsmith observing the *poṣadha* vows should fashion a trident out of *aśvattha* wood, endowed with all the proper characteristics, and having consecrated it with the *sapāta-abhihūta* rite, [one should worship it] on the full moon day with fragrant scents.

Having smeared [the ground] according to one's means and having performed worship before the cloth painting (*paṭa*), one should practice throughout the entire night with the right hand until it blazes. When it blazes, one becomes Mahādeva;
one becomes the lord of spirits (*bhūtādhipati*), a tamer of the difficult-to-tame, and unimpeded among all beings. Having entered the ocean...
One should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times. From the ocean onwards, whatever Naga king one desires, one beholds him; or he gives a jewel-gem (*maṇiratna*).
By taking that, one becomes a Vidyādhara. One becomes the king of all Nāgas and Vidyādharas.
During the fortnight of miracles (*prātihārakapakṣa*), one who observes the *poṣadha* vows should have a copper vessel made by a smith.

Having performed a grand worship on the full moon day and established [the image] before the cloth painting, one should recite the mantra until it blazes. Then, having placed the hand upon it, whatever one desires, all that appears.
This is the *bhadraghaṭa* (auspicious jar) sādhana. Having descended into a river flowing toward the ocean, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times. In which...

Having fashioned a *caitya* out of clay or sand on the full moon day, having installed the cloth-painting (*paṭa*) right there and performed a great worship, one should take hold of a crystal, gem, or clay [image] with the right hand and, seated in the cross-legged posture (*paryaṅka*), recite the mantra until it blazes. One becomes a *vidyādhara* who possesses the wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*).
It happens as follows: having installed a cloth painting in a shrine containing relics, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times.

On the full moon day of the fortnight of miracles, having performed worship according to the ritual rules and having arranged a magnificent garland of lamps, one should take hold of a banner draped with white cloth with the right hand and recite it until it blazes.
One becomes a *vidyādhara* of the banner, unimpeded everywhere. On the full moon day during the fortnight of miracles (*prātihārakapakṣa*),

having performed a great worship before the cloth painting (*paṭa*), one should smear a book of the Blessed Lady *Prajñāpāramitā* with fragrant scents, wrap it with garlands of fragrant flowers, and hold it with the left hand.

Seated in the paryaṅka posture, one should recite [the mantra] until it blazes; then one becomes a king of the vidyādharas. One goes wherever one desires and practices the conduct of a bodhisattva. Having bathed and adorned a beautiful maiden, and having performed worship before the cloth painting according to one's means, one should take hold of her with the left hand.

Standing there, one should recite the mantra until it blazes; by means of that very [blazing], one becomes a *vidyādhara* together with her. Placing one’s hand upon a solitary *liṅga*, one should recite until companions do not see [the practitioner].

One becomes invisible to all accomplished masters (*siddhas*), unapproachable, and gains the power of disappearance. On the thirteenth day, during a lunar or solar eclipse, one should place yellow orpiment behind a leaf of the Bodhi tree and recite the mantra at a shrine containing relics in a temple of Maheśvara until it emits smoke. Having applied this as a forehead mark (*tilaka*), one becomes invisible.
Subsisting on milk and barley gruel, one should recite [the mantra] one thousand times at the three junctions of the day for seven nights at the foot of a tree on the seashore.

One will see jewels belonging to the ocean and may take them as desired. Subsisting on mung beans, one should ascend a mountain peak and recite eight thousand times for twenty nights; [one will obtain] the maṇi-jewels found on the mountains.
A vision occurs. Then, having placed [the object] on his hand and head, one should sit upon it and recite the mantra eight thousand times.
Thus for seven days; he becomes submissive.

Desiring to bring under one's control a king or a high official, one should fashion an image of him from beeswax and cast it into smokeless embers; after seven nights, he becomes submissive. One desiring clothes should take white flowers that have not been crushed, recite the mantra over them once, and cast them into water for seven nights.

One obtains a pair of garments worth eight thousand [pieces of gold]. Having recited the mantra eight thousand times over cow’s ghee, one may take it from a woman; she becomes free of all pain. Anointed with butter over which the mantra has been recited eight hundred times, one may enter fire and will not be burned. Anointed with that same substance, one may enter water and remains immobilized. While reciting the mantra, one may beg for alms as much as one desires.

He consumes [the enemy]. Having fashioned an iron sword the size of a span, having installed the cloth painting in a reliquary containing relics, and having performed a grand worship, one should place the sword upon *aśvattha* leaves that curl to the right and recite the mantra until it blazes. When it has been grasped by him, he flies up together with his retinue.

Surrounded by thousands of *vidyādharas* and invincible to all *vidyādharas*, he lives for ten million years. Having performed the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*), on the eighth or fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, having performed a grand worship of the cloth painting (*paṭa*) and fed the monks designated for the community, [he should draw] a lotus upon realgar ground.

Having drawn a hundred-petaled lotus and seated oneself upon the pericarp of that lotus, one should recite the mantra until the lotus rises up, piercing through the earth. Then, twenty *vidyādharas* appear, seated upon the petals of the lotus. Surrounded by them, one flies upward. One travels together with as many beings as one sees, and those who see one. And he—

The lotus becomes adorned with many jewels. One lives for an eon (*vimāturakalpa*). When the body is cast off, one assumes a form according to one’s own wish. By reciting [the mantra] eight thousand times over a dry tree, it will bloom and bear fruit. Having descended into a shallow stream, one should recite [the mantra]; it becomes water. One should recite it when crossing a river; [the river] becomes dry land.
(From PDF 126, p.

671) One who desires to bring a king or a high official under one's control should, beginning on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, offer eight thousand flowers before the cloth painting (paṭa) and perform eight thousand oblations of salt. This will certainly succeed.

The king becomes submissive. Beginning from that very eighth day, one should recite [the mantra] eight hundred times with *gorocanā* at the three junctions of the day until the eleventh day. Having made a forehead mark (*tilaka*) with it, whomever one looks upon becomes submissive. If one desires to bring a boy or a girl under one's control, one should [offer] eight thousand *siddhārthaka* seeds before the cloth painting (*paṭa*).

One should perform oblations. Having taken the foot-dust of those [women] and fashioned an effigy, whoever one mentions by name becomes subject to one's will. One desiring rain should take cow’s ghee and, during a lunar or solar eclipse, place it in a copper vessel; one should recite the mantra until the threefold accomplishment occurs—namely, when it begins to steam, when it smokes, and when it bursts into flames.
This one possesses the power of retaining what he hears; whatever he hears, he grasps. While [the substance] is smoking, it is a elixir of mercury.
When it is blazing, one becomes a rememberer of past lives (*jātismara*). One should offer a hundred thousand *arka* flowers into the fire; he bestows a hundred thousand *dīnāra*s.
In front of the cloth painting (*paṭa*), one should present eight thousand *arka* flowers; one obtains a hundred *dīnāra*s.

In front of the cloth painting (*paṭa*), one should offer eight thousand oblations of *śāli* rice grains smeared with ghee; one will obtain five *dīnāras*. Having performed the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*), one should offer eight thousand oblations of curds, honey, and ghee in front of the cloth painting; one will obtain three hundred *dīnāras*. One should offer eight thousand oblations of black sesame seeds.
One obtains more than a hundred dīnāras.

Desiring to bring a patriarch (*kulapati*) under one's control, one should offer eight thousand oblations of *arka* wood before the cloth painting (*paṭa*) at the three junctions of the day for seven nights; the patriarch will become submissive. Desiring to bring a lord of the world (*lokapati*) under one's control, one should offer eight thousand oblations of young *dūrvā* shoots before the cloth painting at the three junctions of the day for seven nights.

One attains the status of a Kaula leader for as long as one lives. By one desiring to bring the Noble Saṅgha under control, one should offer eight thousand *arka* flowers before the cloth painting for seven nights; one will find whatever object one seeks. Through constant recitation, one obtains wealth. One should offer eight thousand pellets of *guggulu* incense before the cloth painting.

One obtains a thousand gold pieces. One should offer eight thousand *kunduru* incense sticks before the cloth painting for seven nights; one obtains a treasure-store. One should offer three thousand oblations at the three junctions of the day before the cloth painting, using *arka* wood fuel-sticks smeared with curd, honey, and ghee; one obtains a thousand *dīnāra* coins.

For the subjugation of enemies, one who observes the *poṣadha* vows should offer oblations of royal mustard seeds before the painting at the three junctions of the day for seven days. One will become beloved by all people.

One should offer eight thousand oblations of *śāli* rice grains at the three junctions of the day for seven days. One will obtain one hundred *kārṣāpaṇa* coins. Having performed the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*), on the eighth or fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should take a corpse with its limbs intact, bathe it, adorn it, and worship it with fragrant flowers and incense.
Having stepped upon his chest with the left foot, he should be struck on the head; then he rises. He should be struck with a sword made of *puṣpaloha* (flower-metal);
one obtains gold (*jātarūpa*). If he does not wish [to give it], one should say: "Vomit! Then the *cintāmaṇi* emerges. Having placed it on one's head or neck, or having tied it elsewhere, whatever—

When one thinks of it, it appears. Beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight, having fasted for a day and night, one should descend into a river flowing to the ocean with water reaching to the shoulders and cast ten thousand *jāti* flowers into the current.
One obtains ten *māṣakas*, or a thousand pieces of gold. Beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight, [one should do this] at a river flowing to the ocean...
One should offer ten thousand lotuses into a river for seven nights; one obtains a collection of hidden treasures.

Having performed the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*), one should descend into that same river and cast ten thousand flowers into the current for seven days; one obtains ten villages. Furthermore, having made a pill the size of a chickpea from *aśoka* flowers...

Before the cloth painting, one should offer eight thousand oblations at the three junctions of the day for seven nights, using fuel sticks of *apāmārga* smeared with curd, honey, and ghee. Whomever one seeks, that person one obtains. This is the procedure: by means of *apāmārga* grains mixed with *aśoka* pills, one obtains a thousand pieces of gold before the cloth painting.

One should offer ten thousand oblations of ghee while reciting the name [of the person]; within one month, one obtains a princess. One who desires to bring a king together with his ministers under control should kindle a fire before a cloth painting (*paṭa*) using *aśoka* wood fuel, and [offer] ten [thousand oblations] of *aśoka* flowers smeared with curd, honey, and ghee.

One should offer oblations by the thousands; that practitioner will come under one's control. Having kindled a fire before a painted image, one should offer ten thousand oblations of *apāmārga* wood and *śatapuṣpā* flowers smeared with curd, honey, and ghee.
One will see a treasure in one's own house. Having descended into a river flowing to the ocean until the water reaches the waist...

One should offer ten thousand [oblations]. Those who smell them [attain success]. Having formed a fist with the left hand, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times; one becomes accomplished (*siddha*). Upon releasing [the fist], it becomes visible. Having installed the cloth-painting (*paṭa*) at a shrine containing relics, on a riverbank, or on a mountain, one should offer one hundred thousand lotuses as a fire-oblation (*homa*); one beholds Śrī. By this very same procedure...

One should offer one hundred thousand blue lotuses; one sees all manner of things. One should offer one hundred thousand pills of guggulu resin; one obtains ten million gold pieces. One should offer one hundred thousand fragrant flowers;
one obtains ten million garments. By means of guggulu incense, even with eight recitations, one fulfills whatever one has requested.
(From *pdf* 128, p.
673) One should offer eight thousand oblations of sesame and mustard seeds before the cloth painting (*paṭa*) every day for three days.
One obtains twenty-five *dīnāras*. By this very same procedure, one should offer oblations for seven nights; [one will obtain] one hundred *dīnāras*.

One obtains [the desired result]. Having cut a salt image again and again, one should offer it into the fire eight thousand times; whoever one desires, whether woman or man, becomes submissive. For three days, one should offer eight thousand mustard seeds moistened with both hands and smeared with ghee; this pacifies all obstacles. Having placed one foot in the water...

On dry land, one should recite the mantra alone until the foot that was in the water becomes light; then one becomes liberated from sin. Having kindled a fire with *arka* wood, one should offer eight thousand oblations of mustard seeds for seven days;
the karmic obstructions will be exhausted. One should prepare equal parts of the powder of *brāhmī*, *guḍūcī*, and *pippalī*.

Having recited [the mantra] twenty-one times over honey in the presence of Mañjuśrī, one should lick it for seven nights; one becomes intelligent. For fourteen nights, one becomes supremely intelligent. By practicing this for two months, one becomes a possessor of a retentive memory (*śrutidhara*).
Having performed eight thousand recitations before a painted image or a statue, one should afterwards drink it. Thus...

Reciting it silently day after day, one becomes wise. Whether bound or imprisoned, one is released by the recitation alone. Upon seeing thieves, one should recite; one will not be robbed by thieves. Having consecrated oil eight thousand times with the mantra, one should smear it on the head;
one will become beloved by all people. Those who touch [the image] in front of the Blessed Buddha will all become submissive.
With this very mantra, one should anoint the wound of a person struck by a weapon with oil consecrated eight thousand times;

the wound will vanish and no pain will arise. Having recited this over a clod of earth seven times, one should throw it into water; thus the mouths of crocodiles, turtles, and other such creatures are bound. On the full moon day, having fasted for three nights—
Having entered the water up to the navel, one should offer eight hundred white flowers;
one will obtain a pair of garments worth five dīnāras. During a lunar eclipse, at a shrine containing relics, one should prepare pills from finely ground *guñjā* powder mixed with ghee and honey.
Having covered [the object] with seven *aśvattha* leaves and shielding it with one's hand, one should recite [the mantra] until it blazes.
One who consumes it becomes a possessor of the power of hearing (*śrutidhara*). By means of this, one should perform rites for all the afflicted.
Having consecrated oil with this [mantra], one who applies it for colic, burning sensations, hemorrhoids, dysuria, old age, or sciatica becomes free from disease.

Beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight, having fasted for three nights, one should offer one hundred thousand oblations of *yūthikā* buds smeared with ghee, curd, and milk beneath an *aśvattha* tree. This destroys [the effects of] *rūpaka*, *piśāca*, fever, spirits, and planetary grahas; it releases [the afflicted] by means of a thread.
For a woman who is unable to give birth, one should recite [the mantra] over oil one hundred and eight times and smear it on her navel or the region of her hips;
she will become free from the obstruction. By holding a clod of earth over which the *anantā* and *vetasī* [mantras] have been recited one hundred times, one should perform the *kumbhīra-dhāraṇa*.

One should recite over *brāhmī*, *vacā*, and *bṛhatī* mixed with honey at a reliquary (*caitya*) containing relics until one sees the moon; [the medicine] will then throb. Having consumed it, one becomes a possessor of the power of hearing (*śrutidhara*). In battle, having consecrated a *pratisarā* cord one hundred and eight times and tied a knot on the wrist, one’s strength remains unassailable.

Having fasted for a day and night, one should accomplish [the rite] in the presence of the Blessed One. Having gone down to a river that flows into the ocean and observed a fast for a fortnight while subsisting on milk and barley gruel, one should offer blooming white lotuses into the water. One sees a treasure-trove. Then, having performed the purification of the body with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya),...

Having performed the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) starting from the first day of the waxing moon until the full moon, and having fasted for three nights at the conclusion, one should take a thread spun by a young girl. Having consecrated it ten thousand times, one should bind it around the wrist at a shrine containing relics (*sadhātuka-caitya*), before an image, or in one's own home; thus one becomes invisible. [Furthermore,] at a shrine containing relics, [one should place] a cloth-painting (*paṭa*).

Having established [the deity], one should offer oblations with thirty thousand lotuses. Having kindled the fire with charcoal from *khadira* wood, one sees [the deity] in its own form. Whatever one seeks, that one obtains. Beginning on the first lunar day and continuing until the fifteenth, having fasted for three nights and performed a magnificent worship at a reliquary (*caitya*) containing relics, [one should use] fuel-sticks of *udumbara* wood.

Having kindled a fire, one should offer oblations of clarified butter; one obtains a village. On the bank of a river flowing toward the ocean, one should cause a thousand stūpas to be constructed. Having offered perfumes, flowers, incense, and so forth to each stūpa daily, one should have them consecrated with eight thousand recitations until the final stūpa blazes. Then it should be known [that success has been attained].

The Blessed One approaches as a great bodhisattva. As he approaches, the earth trembles and fragrant scented winds blow. One should recite the mantra until he stands before one in his own form. Whatever boon one requests, that one obtains. In front of the Blessed One, one should offer eight thousand oblations of pieces of *khadira* wood.
One receives one dīnāra every day. Having gone to Aṭarvī, subsisting on alms, one should offer twenty thousand oblations of forest cow-dung smeared with curd, honey, and ghee.
When the tree deity arrives having assumed the form of a lion, he offers a treasure-trove (nidāna). One must not accept it.

"Come to me yourself," he says; [the deity] then bestows a kingdom, wealth, or other jewels. One must constantly provide enjoyments for the use of the Three Jewels. Having retired to a forest, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times.
One should recite it one hundred thousand times. Again, one should recite it one hundred thousand times before an image of the Blessed One made of agalloch wood.

One should offer seven thousand oblations of the dung of calves mixed with honey, ghee, and sugar. Then a tawny cow (*kapilā*) will appear as a wish-fulfilling cow (*kāmadhenu*). If she does not come, one should again offer twenty thousand oblations of the dung of calves.

And having arrived, she becomes accomplished (*siddhā*). She yields milk for a thousand men. In front of the cloth painting (*paṭa*), one should offer eight thousand *jātī* flowers smeared with ghee and honey. For six months...

One obtains a thousand *dīnāras* or six thousand. One should offer a hundred thousand blossoming lotuses smeared with curds, honey, and ghee at a reliquary (*caitya*) containing relics; the deities who have faith in the Buddha will then grant boons. Having performed worship to the noble Mañjuśrī, [one should offer] white mustard seeds...

One should scatter seven [seeds] consecrated with mantras during battle; peace will prevail. On the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Pratihāraka, having performed worship with perfumes and flowers, one should offer eight thousand oblations of blooming lotuses smeared with ghee. Then, taking the ashes, one should apply a tilaka mark on one's own forehead.

Having performed [the rite], one should enter a village or city; all will become submissive. Starting from the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight until the fifteenth, having stayed for one night, one should smear a mandala measuring four cubits beneath a tree, offer perfumes, flowers, and incense, and perform worship to the noble Mañjuśrī.

Having offered an oblation to the yakṣas and taken human bone, one should have a trident fashioned. Having cast it with the left hand, one who has fasted for either seven nights or three nights should offer eight thousand *jātī* flowers. By that means, the trident blazes; then one becomes accomplished (*siddha*). Whatever one creates by will, that one obtains—a divine house.

During an eclipse of the moon or sun, at a shrine containing relics, or before an image, one should take a *pala* of cow’s ghee from a tawny cow whose calf is of the same color, place it in a golden vessel, perform worship to the Blessed One,
and while not looking at the moon, cover it with a cloth and recite the mantra until it becomes warm, froths, and blazes.
By drinking it while it is steaming, one gains power over all beings; by drinking it while it is foaming, one becomes invisible;
by drinking it while it is flaming, one travels through the sky.

For one who has performed the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) for six months, subsisting on cow’s urine and barley gruel, observing a vow of silence, and reciting the mantra constantly, [the goal] is obtained without having to beg.

One obtains a hundred gold pieces. Beginning with the fortnight of the gatekeeper (pratihāraka-pakṣa), having performed worship before the Blessed One, the Noble Mañjuśrī, for one year while offering perfumes, flowers, and so forth, and being endowed with the eightfold poṣadha vows, one becomes successful when the year is complete. The Blessed One [confers] this upon him.

One performs the binding of the turban. Having performed worship to Noble Mañjuśrī, beginning from the first lunar day until the full moon day, one should perform increasingly greater worship day by day. One should also feed the monks. When the words "I have attained success" issue forth, one should offer one hundred thousand oblations of ghee; thus peace is brought to another.

On the day of the *pratihāraka*, having performed a magnificent worship of the Buddha and of the noble Mañjuśrī with perfumes, flowers, lamps, incense, and so forth, one should offer one hundred thousand oblations of *śaṅkhapuṣpī* flowers soaked in pure oil.

676) There will be villages, cities, elephants, horses, chariots, cows, and buffaloes. Having observed the *poṣadha* for seven nights and subsisting on milk and barley-gruel, one should fill a bowl with clarified butter strained [of impurities] and light a lamp with a white wick.
One should show it to boys and girls; there, one sees that even those of little knowledge have attained perfection.

There will be no fear from any calamities. One who constantly recites the mantra should offer eight thousand oblations of ghee-soaked fuel-sticks from the Bodhi tree. Likewise, one should sleep before the cloth painting on a bed of *kuśa* grass.

In a dream, one sees twenty thousand pieces of wealth; one portion of this wealth is to be dedicated to the Three Jewels. Beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight until the full moon, during this interval, one should recite the mantra eight thousand times every day. Having performed worship with perfumes, flowers, incense, and so forth, at the conclusion, one who has fasted for three nights [should proceed].

Observe the vow of silence and recite the mantra. Having placed an offering (*bali*) in your hand for the obstructing spirits (*prāticāraka*), go to the great road and announce the cruel spirit. You should say, "May he accept. Taking one *droṇa* of white mustard seeds, scatter them toward the ten directions and downward. After consecrating [the seeds] twenty-one times, [protect] yourself and others.

One should reveal it. Likewise, on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, having entered the Gandhakuṭī, one should recite [the mantra] a thousand times before the Blessed One. Having performed the offering of oblations with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one then sees the Blessed Noble Mañjuśrī in a dream. This should be done by one observing the *poṣadha* vows during the dark fortnight of the month of Vaiśākha.
Subsisting on a diet of milk and barley-gruel, one should perform worship with perfumes, flowers, lamps, and so forth at a reliquary containing relics;
furthermore, monks should be fed day after day. Four water-jars filled with water and containing all medicinal herbs and seeds should be placed [there] by the monks during the night.
Having consecrated each one eight thousand times with mantras, one should place it where there is no crowing of crows, near a son, a wife, or a daughter; [this secures] sovereignty.

On the eighth day of the dark fortnight within the two fortnights, having performed worship to the Blessed One and to the noble Mañjuśrī, and having kindled a fire in a cremation ground, one should offer eight thousand *śatapuṣpa* flowers as an oblation.

Food and drink become inexhaustible. Taking that very ash and making a sectarian mark (*puṇḍraka*) on the forehead of oneself or another, if one enters into battle, all [enemies] will come under one's control; one shall also be released from bondage and fetters. It destroys [the power of] fire. [One should offer] *mālatī* flowers smeared with curd, honey, and ghee...

One should offer a hundred thousand oblations. Subsisting on cow urine for six months, one obtains a thousand dīnāras. Beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight, one should offer eight thousand blue lotuses; whoever’s name one offers them for becomes submissive. Whoever’s name one offers eight thousand [oblations] of *pañcakālaka* flowers at the three junctions of the day, that person...

One becomes submissive. On the fortnight of miracles (prātihārakapakṣa), subsisting on milk and barley gruel, one should recite [the mantra] three times daily before the cloth painting on the fifteenth day, until the Blessed One arrives; the flame of the lamp increases and the earth trembles.

The cloth moves, or the words "it is accomplished" issue forth; one obtains a thousand *dīnāras* and becomes the lord of a province. [This occurs] for one who has performed the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) for six months before the Blessed One, Noble Mañjuśrī, at a shrine containing relics.

Within six months, one obtains five thousand dīnāras. Having performed worship at a reliquary containing relics (*sadhātuka-caitya*), one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times; one obtains eight thousand gold coins (*rūpaka*). One should recite it one hundred thousand times at a reliquary containing relics; one becomes the foremost in all desires. It is a pacifier of all diseases.
One who desires to perform this rite should empower a thread spun by a maiden with one hundred and eight thousand recitations and tie it on;

he will obtain good fortune, and his illnesses will be pacified. Having descended to a river flowing to the ocean, one should offer eight thousand black sesame seeds at a shrine containing relics (*sadhātuka-caitya*); one will obtain wealth and grain.

Beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight, having fasted for three nights until the fifteenth day, one should kindle a fire with *udumbara* wood and offer one hundred thousand oblations of royal mustard seeds smeared with curd, honey, and ghee.
One obtains five villages. Having kindled a fire with fuel-sticks of the *rājavṛkṣa* tree, [one should offer] white sesame seeds...

One should offer one hundred thousand oblations of sesame seeds smeared with curd, honey, and ghee. Having fasted for three nights on the fifteenth day, if those sesame seeds travel in all directions and intermediate directions, then one becomes accomplished (*siddha*). One brings all sentient beings under one's control.
First, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times before the noble Mañjuśrī; thereafter, during a lunar eclipse...
Having offered eight *palas* of clarified butter, one should recite [the mantra] until it begins to foam; having drunk it, one becomes a listener of wisdom (*śrutadhara*).

One should offer *kunduruka* incense one hundred thousand times; then one obtains one ancient [object] without asking. One should present eight hundred fragrant flowers every day before the noble Mañjuśrī.

One becomes illustrious. One should offer eight thousand oblations daily of *apāmārga* fuel-sticks smeared with curd, honey, and ghee; one obtains a village. Having kindled the fire with *bahuputrikā* fuel-sticks, one should offer eight thousand oblations of *vacā*; by making a forehead mark (*tilaka*) with those ashes, one becomes invisible. If [it does not happen]...

If it does not happen, one should perform it three times. Having gone to the bank of a river during a lunar eclipse, having kindled a fire with *bilva* fuel-sticks, one should offer one hundred thousand *bilva* flowers smeared with ghee. A young Yakṣa maiden arrives.
At midnight, having again recited the mantra eight thousand times, then one [maiden] comes. Whatever word is spoken, that...

One performs [the rite]. At the site of the treasure, one should recite the mantra eight thousand times after having performed worship with flowers, incense, perfumes, and so forth. Then, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, having performed the offering of the bali, one should recite. The piśācas arrive. Then one should dig. The treasure rises up. Having taken it, one should give it to oneself and to the Three Jewels. Thus...

The act of binding the turban is also a ritual procedure. Having kindled a fire with *vibhītaka* wood in front of the Blessed One, one should offer eight thousand oblations of sesame seeds and rice daily.

A widow becomes submissive. To subjugate ministers, one should offer oblations of white mustard seeds; they will become submissive. To subjugate a king, one should offer oblations of resinous incense (*sarjarasa*); he will become submissive. To subjugate men and women, one should offer this very same substance. Having kindled a fire with *agasti* wood, one should [offer] lamp-wicks before the painting for a hundred *dīnāras*.
O Blessed One, one should offer oblations of *palāśa* wood fuel with milk as the sacrificial substance three times every day.

One will obtain a hundred gold pieces. Having gone to a river flowing to the ocean, one should offer oblations a hundred thousand times; one should take hold of whatever jewels are obtained. A portion to be used for the Three Jewels must be given away.

On the full moon day of Vaiśākha, one should recite [the mantra] for the entire night; one is liberated from the [five] immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*). Having performed worship of the Blessed One, the Noble Mañjuśrī, at the foot of the Bodhi tree, one should offer oblations of *apāmārga* wood chips smeared with curd, honey, and ghee, dedicated to oneself; one becomes liberated from all sins. Seven...
Having consecrated seven *marica* peppers with mantras, one should eat them when there is no crowing of crows; one will then grasp five thousand verses (*śloka*).

One retains that [retention] for as long as one lives. Having performed one hundred thousand recitations before the Blessed Buddha, one effects the binding of *pannaga* serpents. Or, [one may do so] with *vaikaṅkata* fuel-sticks in water.

One should offer one hundred thousand oblations of items smeared with curd, honey, and ghee before the noble Mañjuśrī; at midnight, one obtains five hundred dīnāras, half of which is to be dedicated to the Three Jewels. One should offer eight thousand white water lilies day after day; one will be liberated from the Vināyakas during the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika.

Subsisting on milk and barley-gruel, or subsisting on vegetables, observing the *poṣadha* vows, and having fasted for three nights on the fifteenth day, one should offer a hundred thousand oblations of *vaikaṅkata* fruits smeared with ghee. One obtains a thousand gold coins and becomes the lord of a village; half of this is for the use of the Three Jewels. On a clean plot of ground the size of a cow-hide...
Having smeared the mandala and constructed an altar in the shape of a lotus in its center,

and having prepared an offering of various fragrances, flowers, incense, and bali, one should offer a hundred thousand oblations of fuel-sticks made of *vaikaṅkata* wood, each measuring one span of the Sugata. Blue-colored flames in the shape of fire will issue forth, and after circumambulating the practitioner, they will [return].
Again, they enter the fire-pit; in this way, one becomes accomplished. In all ritual practices (*sādhana*), fire must be invoked;

in this way, one becomes accomplished. Having descended into the Ganges until the water reaches the armpits, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times until the solar disc is seen in the sky. Then the Blessed One becomes accomplished. If one does not see it—

Success is not achieved by going [there] only once; rather, having performed the offering of perfumes, flowers, incense, and bali, one should recite the mantra throughout the entire night until dawn. Then, one becomes accomplished. This [practice] must not be disclosed regarding any other ritual accomplishments (*sādhana*).
"He gives me a hundred coins day after day, provided I spend it all; otherwise, he does not give.

One should kindle a fire with *palāśa* wood and offer eight thousand oblations of wild cow-dung smeared with curds, honey, and ghee. One obtains a hundred cows. One should offer eight thousand oblations of *mātuluṅga* fruits.

In a fire of *palāśa* wood, [one should worship] until Gaṇapati arrives. He should be addressed: "Give me one *dīnāra* every day. When he gives it, all of it must be spent. He should be told, "Touch the feet of the Blessed One," and then success is attained. Alternatively, if he does not give, [one should offer] *bilva* fruits smeared with curd, honey, and ghee at a reliquary (*caitya*) containing relics.
Having stayed for one night before the cloth painting, one should kindle a fire with *vaikaṅkata* wood and offer eight thousand oblations.

By this rite, one becomes glorious and becomes the lord of a realm. [Using] *kiṅkirāṭa* flowers, by this rite one becomes glorious and becomes the lord of a realm. [Offering] *kiṅkirāṭa* flowers day after day...

One should offer eight thousand oblations for seven days; one obtains eight *paṇas*. One who wishes to perform a rite of pacification (*śāntika*) should offer eight thousand oblations of parched grain (*lāja*); peace shall prevail. One desiring prosperity (*puṣṭi*) should kindle a fire with fuel-sticks of milky trees and offer eight thousand oblations of sesame seeds and rice at the three junctions of the day.

One should perform oblations for three days; prosperity will ensue. Having kindled a fire with mango wood, one should offer eight thousand sprouts of *dūrvā* grass; in a dispute, one becomes the winner. At sunset, having taken the name [of the person], one should offer rice husks with the left hand; within seven nights, that person becomes submissive.

Having kindled the fire with *rājasamit* fuel-sticks, one should offer eight thousand oblations of sesame seeds and rice at the three junctions of the day for three days; he will grant wealth. On the banks of the Gaṅgā, in a pure place free from the sound of pestles, one should take earth from both banks and construct a square altar seven cubits in size, in the center of which—
Having fashioned a thousand-petaled lotus and placed upon it a fivefold red wheel measuring one span of a Sugata,
one should accomplish the rite in the center of the maṇḍala before the cloth painting; having worshipped with perfumes,
flowers, and white sandalwood, and having offered a garland of mandārava and red flowers, one should then perform worship with perfumes and other offerings.

Having prepared a garland of ghee lamps, seven should be offered in the four directions, and four jars of ghee should be set ablaze. In the four directions, four vases filled with all kinds of seeds should be placed, having cast jewels into them. Incense made of kunduru, agaru, śrīpiṣṭaka, and guggulu should be offered.
Having performed the bali-offering in the four directions, one should offer rice mixed with curd and cakes as previously described.

To the south, one should offer meat mixed with water. In the western direction, one should offer a vessel filled with jaggery and milk. In the northern direction, one should present a bali-offering filled with milk-rice (pāyasa).
Then, having kindled the fire with *palāśa* fuel-sticks,

one should offer eight thousand oblations of clarified butter over which seven recitations of the *apāmārga* fuel-sticks have been performed, while uttering the name [of the person] to be brought under control (*vaśīkaraṇa*).

It comes to pass: having kindled a fire with *rājavṛkṣa* wood and fashioned an image out of salt, one should offer eight thousand oblations—one for each syllable of the name, beginning from the head down to the feet—each oblation consecrated seven times while reciting the name. The king becomes submissive. This should be done on the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight or on the eighth.
Having observed the *poṣadha* vow and remained awake for a full day and night, one should take unfallen cow dung and smear a sacrificial ground the size of a cow-hide.

Then, at a shrine containing relics, one should take fresh butter churned by a maiden from the milk of a tawny cow that has a calf of the same color, using a silver vessel belonging to the noble Mañjuśrī. Finally, one should sit down upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass.

Holding the vessel with the left hand, one should stir it with the ring finger and the thumb of the right hand while reciting the mantra until it becomes warm. That [liquid] should be drunk; one will then become wise and will grasp what is said only once.
If it smokes, there is subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*). If it blazes, invisibility (*antardhāna*) occurs. [One obtains] many children.

One should perform eight thousand oblations. With that ash, one should prepare four water-pots by mixing them together. Having consecrated a mantra eight hundred times, one should bind it upon the right hand; thereby, one becomes a superior debater everywhere. One should also offer eight thousand oblations of *aparājita* flowers.

One becomes unconquered in battle. One should make knots with thread spun by a maiden that has been consecrated seven times; these should be tied [on the body]. Neither stationary nor moving poisons have power here. For one bitten by a fierce serpent, one should take the name [of the victim] and give water mixed with powder consecrated seven times for them to drink.

Even one who is dead shall rise up. Likewise, having consecrated [the substance] four times with mantras, it should be given for drinking; even one bitten by Takṣaka survives. One should smear the breasts and the cheeks with earth consecrated seven times; [the person] is liberated, and no pain occurs. During an epidemic or calamity, one should smear a sacrificial ground in the middle of the city at midnight.

Having offered a white *bali* and kindled the fire with fuel-sticks of milk-tree wood, one should offer a thousand oblations of milk. This pacifies the plague. If it is not pacified, then on another day at the time of midday, having kindled the fire with fuel-sticks of *śleṣmātaka* wood, one should offer eight thousand oblations of white mustard seeds (*siddhārtha*). Immediately...

It pacifies pestilence. When this rite is performed, those beings who are bound by adverse forces come under his control. For the subjugation of *kūṣmāṇḍa* spirits, one should offer eight thousand oblations of *kūṣmāṇḍa* wood; it pacifies pestilence. For the subjugation of *preta* spirits, one should offer eight thousand oblations of sesame flour.
Pretas become submissive. For the subjugation of piśācas, one should offer eight thousand oblations of rags from a cemetery;
the piśācas will become submissive. For the subjugation of birds, one should offer eight thousand oblations of fuel-sticks from the vaṭa tree smeared with curd, honey, and ghee.

681) Yakṣas become submissive. For the subjugation of epilepsy, *ujjehāra*, and *vaśīkarana*, one should offer eight thousand oblations of wool (*ūrṇā*). Yakṣas become submissive. [For the subjugation of] epilepsy, *ujjehāra*, and *vaśīkarana*.

One should offer eight thousand oblations of wool; [the targets] become submissive. One should offer eight thousand oblations of guggulu resin pills smeared with clarified butter; the planetary spirits who follow Mahādeva become submissive.
Having taken realgar purchased from a hero, one should kindle a fire with fuel-sticks of the *rājavṛkṣa* tree and recite the mantra that many times.

When it has reached the color of fire, one should then extinguish it in the clarified butter (*ghṛta*) produced from the fresh butter (*navanīta*) churned by a maiden from a tawny cow (*kapilā*) that has a calf of the same color. One should do the same with a vessel full of curd and a vessel full of honey.

Then, having performed protection (*rakṣā*) with this very [mantra] and placed it in a casket, one should [perform the rite] during a lunar eclipse, having fasted for three nights, together with the relics (*sadhātuka*).

Having performed worship before the Caitya of Noble Mañjuśrī, one should place [the substance] upon four leaves of the *aśvattha* tree while facing north and recite the mantra until it becomes warm, emits smoke, or blazes forth. [The results are] subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*), invisibility (*antardhāna*), and traveling through the sky (*ākāśagamana*). The same applies to collyrium (*añjana*), yellow orpiment (*haritāla*), and gorocana.

This is the specific procedure for using *rocanā*: on the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight, having placed [the substance] upon a lotus leaf and holding it with cupped hands before the noble Mañjuśrī, one should recite the mantra until the threefold accomplishment is attained.
These rites are to be performed before the primary image (*mūlapaṭa*). Having fashioned a lotus from the five metals over seven nights, [one should proceed].
Having ground saffron, *rocanā*, and camphor in water and smeared it upon a lotus,
one who has observed the fast on the eighth day of the bright fortnight, having bathed three times a day and dressed in clean garments,
should recite the mantra with the lotus held in the right hand before an image of Noble Mañjuśrī containing relics, until it blazes forth.

Then, by taking that [substance], one becomes a Vidyādhara and lives for ten thousand years. Likewise with a bracelet, a crown, or a chain. In the same way, having combined together mountain red sandalwood, guggulu, the root of *nandyāvarta*, the chaff of *girikarṇikā*, rice, costus, tagara, honey, long pepper, and frankincense;

One should have equal portions prepared. Then, having taken the milk of a tawny cow that has a calf of the same color, and having mixed it with butter churned by a maiden, one should form it into pills. A lamp should be offered with unbroken sesame oil. Then, on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight, one who observes the *upoṣadha* vow and has fasted for a full day and night should place the pill between leaves of the *aśvattha* tree.

First, one should recite the mantra in the presence of the noble Mañjuśrī until it emits smoke; having given some to one's companions, one should place [the remainder] in one's own mouth, and one becomes invisible. Then, if it bursts into flames, one becomes a traveler through the sky. Another method:
at a shrine containing relics, in front of the cloth painting (*paṭa*), having performed a magnificent worship while observing the *poṣadha* vows, [one should kindle] a fire with *arka* wood fuel...

Having kindled the fire, one should offer eight thousand oblations of *khadira* wood fuel sticks smeared with curd, honey, and clarified butter, beginning on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight until the fifteenth. One becomes accomplished as soon as the [practice] is perfected. Thus.

One who observes the *poṣadha* vow should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times; thereafter, the ritual actions may be performed. Through this preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*), one becomes accomplished.

Now, if one desires to bring a king or a high official under one's control, one should perform worship of the Blessed One and offer eight thousand oblations of fuel-sticks from the *rājavṛkṣa* tree smeared with *iṅguda* oil.

Starting from the fourteenth day until the fifteenth—by this ritual, even one of immoral conduct attains success. One who desires to bring the four castes under control should fetch milk-rice (*pāyasa*), sacrificial food (*haviṣyānna*), and drinkable *kṛsarā*, and offer them as oblations;
they will become submissive. At night, being pure, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times; it liberates one from all bonds.

For the pacification of anger, one may perform a *piṇḍa* or *tuṣa* homa; for the subjugation of a maiden, one should offer sesame seeds. For the desire of clothing, one should offer *karppaṇa*. Having consecrated *vacā* root eight thousand times, if one binds it to the hand for seven nights and offers it eight thousand times, whatever one asks for, that one obtains through constant recitation.

If one binds the *pratyaṅgirā* [mantra] onto someone’s hand with a lotus fiber or similar material over which it has been consecrated eight thousand times, protection is afforded to that person. One desiring wealth should offer eight thousand oblations of guggulu pills. For seven nights, one desiring to become a leader of a family (*kulapati*) should offer incense smeared with clarified butter for seven nights; he will obtain a village.

If one gives flowers over which the mantra has been recited eight hundred times to someone, that person becomes submissive. Saffron, tagara, tālīśapatra, lotus stalks, śatapuṣpa, and śrīveṣṭa, combined and consecrated according to the ritual procedure, serve as a means of subjugation for men and women when applied as a garland at the king’s gate.

The method for achieving victory in battle: Having consecrated the banner by reciting the mantra eight thousand times, and having empowered perfumes, flowers, and incense, one should offer an *arghya* oblation into seven vessels of curd. By the mere sight of it, the enemy army perishes. Furthermore, having consecrated black sesame seeds eight thousand times before the cloth painting, [one should employ them] with the name of whomever [is targeted].

Having seized it, one consumes it and gains mastery. Having recited [the mantra] eight thousand times over all seeds, all medicinal herbs, all fragrances, and fragrant flowers—or a lotus—one should place them all in a jar of *mūlaka* root that has not yet reached its time [of ripening], and then recite [the mantra] eight thousand times at the Bodhi tree. One may bathe oneself, or cause another to bathe.

One becomes liberated from all calamities. By offering a lotus or a lotus leaf into smokeless embers while reciting the name of someone, that person becomes submissive. One should offer eight thousand *bilva* leaves mixed with honey; this subjugates either the wife of a king or the queen. For the subjugation of all beings, [one should use] *priyaṅgu*.
One should perform the oblation. By taking the name of whomever one offers red śāli rice, that person becomes submissive.
To subjugate a maiden, one should offer kesara flowers. In front of the cloth painting (paṭa), one should offer milk-porridge eight thousand times.

683) He becomes subject to the name of whoever [performs this rite]. Having installed the cloth-painting facing east in a reliquary (*sadhātuka*) shrine, beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight, one should spread out the altar with *darbha* grass whose tips point toward the northeast, and [kindle] the fire with *bilva* fuel-sticks.

Having kindled a fire, one should offer eight thousand oblations at the three junctions of the day using blossomed lotuses smeared with curd, honey, and ghee. Incense made of agaru, turuṣka, kunduruka, and śrīpiṣṭaka should be offered. One should present an offering of milk, curd, and cooked rice, as well as an offering for all spirits to ward off obstacles.

Then, from the eighth day onwards, one should offer eight thousand oblations at the three junctions of the day using blooming white lotuses smeared with curd, honey, and ghee; one will obtain a great treasure or a kingdom. One should offer eight thousand oblations every day using yellow flowers smeared with curd, honey, and ghee; [one will obtain] a country.

One obtains [the result]. Having fasted for three nights and subsisting on a diet of barley meal, one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*). In this manner, even for one who has committed an act of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*), success is achieved through seventy hundred thousand [offerings]. Likewise, one should offer one hundred thousand oblations of fuel-sticks smeared with curd, honey, and ghee; one obtains ten million pieces of gold. Rising at dawn and remaining self-restrained, one should [perform the rite].

Having bathed and observed the vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), one who desires to bring under control a king, a noble, or a high official should kindle a fire and offer eight thousand oblations of *nāgakesara*, *priyaṅgu*, and *rājāna* flowers at the three junctions of the day. Within three months, one obtains distinguished results and abundant wealth. [One may also offer] one hundred thousand cow-dung cakes.

One should offer oblations; one obtains a hundred cows. By offering oblations with *priyaṅgu* and *nāgakesara* fuel-sticks while uttering the name of someone, that person becomes submissive. One should offer eight thousand oblations of *khadira* fuel-sticks smeared with curds, honey, and ghee before the cloth-painting at the three junctions of the day; one obtains a great treasure. That...

What is given becomes inexhaustible. Having descended into a river flowing to the ocean, one should cause a hundred thousand lotuses smeared with red sandalwood to float away; one will see a treasure equal in size to a heap of lotuses.
One should offer eight thousand oblations of *bilva* fruits before the cloth painting (*paṭa*) at the three junctions of the day; this produces enjoyments.
Having combined sesame seeds and rice grains, one should offer eight thousand oblations before the cloth painting at the three junctions of the day for seven nights;
inexhaustible food will then arise. One should offer *nāgapuṣpa* flowers to the *nāgas*; they will become submissive.
To the *yakṣas*, one should offer eight thousand pellets of *guggulu* resin before the cloth painting at the three junctions of the day.

For seven nights, by means of *aśoka* fuel-sticks, a *yakṣiṇī* becomes submissive. One should offer *śrīvāsaka* incense before the cloth painting; the *kinnaras* become submissive. Desiring to bring the gods under one's control, one should offer eight thousand fuel-sticks of *agaru* smeared with ghee before the original cloth painting.
For twenty-one nights at the three junctions of the day, [the targets] become submissive. One should offer *kunduruka* resin before the cloth painting;
the *preta*s become submissive. One should offer *sarjarasa* resin; the *vināyakas* become submissive. By offering oil-cakes (*piṇyāka*), one brings everyone under control.

One who desires to bring a king or a high official under one's control should offer eight thousand oblations of royal mustard seeds smeared with oil before the cloth painting for seven nights. They will become submissive and do whatever they are told.

To bring a princess under one's control, one should offer an oblation of black mustard seeds before the cloth painting. Desiring to subjugate a domestic priest, one should offer clarified butter before the cloth painting. For a kṣatriya, one should use oblations of ghee. To subjugate a vaiśya, one should offer milk.
To subjugate a śūdra, one should offer kṛsarā (rice and sesame mixed with milk). To subjugate all women, one should perform an oblation of salt.

By means of a *māṣa*-oblation, a widow brings all beings under her control when they have been smeared with sesame oil. For all [rites], the oblation consists of eight thousand [offerings] over seven nights. Having become pure and having fasted for four meals, one should kindle a fire with *vilva* fuel-sticks and offer *vilva* fruits; one will see a treasure after one hundred thousand [offerings]. This is for twenty nights.

One who subsists on a diet of milk and barley should offer one hundred thousand oblations of white mustard seeds; he obtains wealth. Having performed the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*), one should offer clarified butter-smeared yellow mustard seeds before the cloth painting for a day and night during the night; within a month, there will be a bountiful rain wherever one desires. One who has fasted for four meals should offer ten thousand oblations of these same seeds.

One obtains wealth. Having installed a cloth painting (*paṭa*) in a reliquary (*caitya*) containing relics, one should kindle a fire with *palāśa* wood and offer a hundred thousand *utpala* flowers; one obtains a village. In front of the painting, while subsisting on milk and barley-gruel, one should offer *gandha*, flowers, and incense, and then offer *padma* lotuses; one obtains a thousand pieces of gold. [With] *kumuda* lotuses...

One should offer one hundred thousand oblations before the cloth painting; whatever one contemplates in the mind, that one obtains. One should offer one thousand oblations of *bilva* fruits before the cloth painting; one beholds a treasure-trove. One should offer one hundred thousand oblations of lotuses smeared with curd, honey, and ghee before the cloth painting, while subsisting on a diet of milk and barley-gruel.

One obtains a thousand gold pieces. Having fasted for three nights, one should offer eight thousand oblations of *agaru* (aloe wood) fuel sticks. Then, a recitation (*jāpa*) must be performed throughout the entire night. The cloth painting (*paṭa*) will tremble, or perhaps the garlands and wreaths will move. Thereupon, it becomes accomplished (*siddha*). Whatever one conceives in the mind, that he bestows. For the subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*) of a great person, [one should offer] *jātī* flowers before the cloth painting.

One should perform oblations. For the purpose of causing discord, one should offer oblations of *karavīra* flowers; one should offer oblations of *karṇikāra* flowers; one obtains a hundred *dīnāras*. One desiring the rank of a general should offer oblations of *kunda* flowers; one obtains the position of a general.
One should offer oblations of *tārāvarta* flowers; one obtains a thousand *dīnāras*. One should offer oblations of a hundred thousand *muculinda* flowers.

One obtains a thousand gold pieces. By offering white *karavīra* flowers into the fire, one becomes bound to the three-footed [seat]. One also obtains a kingdom; having established a sacred fire before the cloth painting (*paṭa*), worship should be performed with increasing intensity every day. One should offer a thousand oblations of gold, each the size of a *tuṭi*, anointed with fragrant oil. Until...
The Blessed One is the Giver of Boons.

685) Thereupon, one becomes a universal monarch of the Vidyādharas. Whatever one prays for, one should offer oblations of silver powder; [one will obtain] a kingdom.

He gives. One should offer an oblation of iron powder; one obtains a thousand *dīnāras*. One should offer a hundred thousand oblations of saffron mixed with fragrant oil; one obtains whatever one prays for. One should offer a hundred thousand oblations of all types of perfumes; one obtains a realm according to one's desire.

One should offer a hundred thousand oblations of camphor; one obtains a hundred thousand dīnāras. One should offer a hundred thousand oblations of sandalwood fuel-sticks smeared with fragrant oil; one obtains a thousand dīnāras. One should offer a hundred thousand oblations of gold and cloth;
one obtains a thousand dīnāras. One should offer a hundred thousand oblations of agalloch wood fuel-sticks; one becomes a possessor of the Vedas (*śrutidhara*).
