It happens as follows: one should offer a hundred thousand oblations of *dhāsaka* wood-fuel smeared with fragrant oil;
there will be the pacification of great diseases. One should offer a hundred thousand oblations of nimba fruits smeared with fragrant oil;
it liberates one from all bonds. Having taken the ghee of a cow that has a calf of the same age, one should drink it after it has been consecrated a hundred thousand times.
One becomes intelligent. One should offer one hundred thousand *arka* flowers; one will become beloved by all beings.

Having consecrated a flower and fruit seven times with mantras, whoever is given it will come under one's control. On the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight, being observant of the *poṣadha* vows, one should smear a mandala with fallen cow dung at a shrine containing relics.

Having performed worship with perfumes, flowers, and lamps of clarified butter, one should kindle a fire with *udumbara* wood and offer eight thousand oblations of *brahmī* fuel-sticks. One who subsists on sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) becomes wise.
To subjugate a Brahmin, one should offer milk; he will become submissive. For a Kṣatriya, one should offer sacrificial food (*haviṣya*).

One becomes [the other's] subordinate. For the subjugation of a Vaiśya, one should offer as an oblation a mixture of barley, curd, and sacrificial food (haviṣya) combined together; he becomes subordinate. Upon seeing an enemy, one should mutter [the mantra]; he is paralyzed. With water consecrated seven times, one fulfills all desires. For all diseases, there is the act of wiping [with it]. One should anoint the eyes with a pellet of *lodhra* wood consecrated seven times.
It removes eye disease. For one who is ill, a thread should be bound after it has been consecrated seven times; all seizing spirits (grahas) will have no power over them.
With ashes over which the mantra has been recited seven times, a protection circle (maṇḍala-bandha) is formed; by binding it upon the topknot (śikhā), self-protection is achieved.

With a clod of earth over which the mantra has been recited seven times, a boundary for the directions (diśā-bandha) is established. For those who suffer from difficult labor and the like, oil should be given after it has been consecrated with the mantra.

She will give birth easily. For a woman with a difficult delivery, at the time of her fertile period, once she has bathed after her menstrual flow, one should empower cow’s milk by reciting the mantra eight hundred times;
having had her prostrate before all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, it should be given to her to drink. She should also be fed fine rice-milk mixed with ghee. From that, [she will obtain] a son.

It brings forth results. Having installed a pleasing cloth painting (paṭa) facing the east, beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight, one should offer eight thousand pellets of guggulu incense every day.

At the three junctions of the day, he grants whatever one desires. Having performed the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*), one should install the cloth painting (*paṭa*) in a reliquary stupa (*caitya* containing relics),
offer perfumes, flowers, incense, and a sacrificial oblation (*bali*), and then, before the painting, [offer] *agaru* wood fuel-sticks the size of a thumb-joint, anointed with *turuṣka* oil.

One should offer oblations three times a day for seven nights; it bestows a kingdom. It grants the state of a *vidyādhara*, invisibility, the power to travel on foot [through the air], or the faculty of retaining all that is heard. Now, one who wishes to accomplish the *gulikā* (pill) should combine *karṇikāra* filaments, *nāgakesara*, white sandalwood, and elephant ichor, and dry them in the shade.
Having made a pill, one should have it ground by a girl wearing clean garments and the like; this should be done under the Puṣya asterism.

Having purified oneself, one should place seven pills wrapped in the three metals into a casket of black agallochum and recite the mantra before the cloth painting until it makes a "khaṭa-khaṭa" sound. Taking that [casket], one should offer one to the Blessed One and place it in his mouth.

Having cast [the offering] into [the fire], he becomes invisible. In front of the cloth painting, one should offer eight thousand oblations of *lakṣa* flowers smeared with curd, honey, and ghee; one will obtain a treasure.
One should offer eight thousand oblations of *kadamba* flowers smeared with curd, honey, and ghee; [all] sentient beings...
[The practitioner becomes] submissive. Having descended to a river flowing toward the ocean, one who has observed the fast should offer eight thousand *kesara* flowers;

he will obtain ten pairs of garments. Before the cloth painting (*paṭa*), one should offer eight thousand *jāti* flowers smeared with curd, honey, and ghee at the three junctions of the day for seven days.

One becomes beloved by all sentient beings. One bestows and obtains a kingdom. One should offer eight thousand oblations of white water-lilies (*kumuda*) smeared with curd, honey, and ghee for seven days; one obtains five kingdoms. For the subjugation of a king, one should offer royal mustard seeds for seven nights. For the subjugation of a Brahmin...
One should offer eight thousand *karaṇṭaka* flowers for seven nights. For the subjugation of a Vaiśya, one should offer eight thousand *saugandhika* flowers for seven nights.
For the subjugation of a Śūdra, one should offer eight thousand [offerings] into the fire for seven nights. [For] a widow...

One should offer eight thousand oblations of *vaikaṅkata* wood for seven nights. Having consecrated yellow pigment (*rocanā*) eight thousand times at a reliquary (*caitya*) containing relics, one should go to the royal court; all [the king's ministers] will become submissive.
One should offer eight thousand oblations of *dūrvā* grass sprouts; there will be peace for another, as well as peace for oneself.

One who desires to accomplish [this] should offer milk as an oblation at the three junctions of the day; peace will ensue. Having placed ghee in a copper vessel before the southern image of Mahādeva, one should recite the mantra a thousand times and present an offering (*bali*) consisting of all kinds of spirits' food. When the ghee begins to move, one becomes successful (*siddha*). By applying a forehead mark (*tilaka*) made from it, one becomes beloved by all people.
Having performed worship of the Blessed One Cāpītābha and the noble Mañjuśrī for the purpose of increasing intelligence,
one should place ghee in either silver or copper and recite the mantra until the threefold accomplishment is attained. That...
Having drunk it, one becomes wise. When it smokes, there is invisibility; when it blazes, there is travel through the sky.
One who desires to master realgar (manaḥśilā) should subsist on milk and barley gruel and recite the mantra one hundred thousand times.
Having fasted for three nights before Mahādeva, one should establish the substance upon seven leaves of the *aśvattha* tree and cover it with three more.

Having offered a *bali* consisting of all-enriching substances, and having performed protection for oneself and one’s companions without restriction, one should recite [the mantra] until the threefold accomplishment is attained. By means of the blazing [mantra], one lives for ten thousand years. Having fashioned a wheel or a trident out of iron, and having performed a grand worship, one should grasp it with the right hand.

Seated cross-legged before the cloth painting, one should recite [the mantra] until it makes a crackling sound or blazes up. Having grasped that [flame], one becomes a *vidyādhara*, and all gods and humans become subject to one's will. One desiring to perform the *aṅgulīsādhana* (finger-attainment) should take earth from both banks of a river and have a finger made from it. That finger [should be placed] before the cloth painting.

Having first established [the deity], one should draw it forth until it arrives; then it becomes accomplished. Whomever one causes to be drawn forth by means of that [accomplished mantra], he comes. One who desires to accomplish *rocanā* (yellow pigment), having performed the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*), should place it before a painted cloth (*paṭa*), offer perfumes, flowers, and incense, and recite the mantra until it blazes. And by means of that which has been accomplished...

He lives for five thousand years. One who desires to accomplish the lotus should fashion a lotus out of red sandalwood, install it before a cloth painting (paṭa) at a shrine containing relics, and, having performed the preliminary rites (puraścaraṇa), recite the mantra while holding it until it blazes. Having grasped it once it has blazed, one becomes a universal monarch (cakravartin) of all the vidyādharas.

The gods who follow Kailāsa become submissive. One becomes invincible to all the Vidyādharas. With water, there is the treatment of poison. By reciting [the mantra] once over one who is possessed by a fever, etc., he is commanded to depart; with it recited once, there is protection for oneself. With water over which the mantra has been recited, there is protection for one's companions. With it recited three times, there is the binding of the directions. With it recited four times, there is the binding of the mandala.

Having fasted for a day and night on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, one should fashion an image of the noble Mañjuśrī using the fallen cow dung of a tawny cow that has a calf of the same color; having placed it facing east and performed a great worship, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times before it. Then the Blessed One will nod his head, or [another sign].
It reveals the signs of accomplishment (*siddhinimitta*). Thereupon, one becomes accomplished; whatever one contemplates, all that one performs.

The Blessed One becomes the bestower of boons; he fulfills every desire. He also declares what is auspicious or inauspicious in dreams. One may employ [the practice] as desired. By reciting it one thousand times in the forenoon, delicious food arises. [This applies to one who is] observing the *poṣadha* vows.
Subsisting on a diet of milk and barley gruel, one should ascend a mountain peak and recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times. A vision will occur, and it will fulfill one's desires.

Before a cloth painting (*paṭa*), one who has performed the preliminary rites (*kṛtapuraścaraṇa*) should offer eight thousand oblations of *kunduru* resin for seven nights; he will become a king over a single region. At the three junctions of the day, one should offer eight thousand grains of rice throughout the entire night;
one obtains a hundred *dīnāras*. Having kindled a fire with *āṭaruṣaka* wood, [one should offer] *āṭaruṣaka* flowers...
One should offer eight thousand oblations of items smeared with ghee; one obtains gold.
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, having fasted for a day and night, one should offer eight thousand oblations of mustard seeds smeared with ghee;
one obtains a thousand gold coins (*rūpaka*), or else a village, before the painted cloth (*paṭa*).
Having kindled a fire with *śleṣmātaka* wood, one should offer a hundred thousand oblations of young *dūrvā* shoots for three nights;
one obtains a thousand cows. One should offer eight thousand *surasī* leaves; one obtains a divine house.
By reciting [the mantra] a hundred thousand times mentally, one obtains a thousand *purāṇas*. One should offer a thousand balls of rice-flour (*śrīpiṣṭaka*) for seven nights.

At the three junctions of the day, one obtains a thousand *dīnāras*. One accomplishes everything according to one's desire and becomes illustrious and fortunate. One should offer red flowers as a *homa* at a river; one will obtain red garments. On the eighth or the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight, in a secluded place on the earth...
Having offered incense, flowers, and perfumes, as well as a garland, beneath a white *arka* tree to the noble Mañjuśrī,
one should recite the mantra eight thousand times. Afterwards, one should have an image of the noble Mañjuśrī made, the size of a thumb-joint,
at a secluded spot on an anthill on the eighth day of the bright fortnight.

One should recite the mantra eight thousand times while offering white perfumes, bali-offerings, garlands, incense, and food oblations. Then, having taken earth from an anthill, one should knead it with scented water. Using that clay, one should fashion a counter-seal (pratimudrā) for the previously made seal of the image by means of the milk of the *arka* plant. Thereafter, beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight until the eighth day, [one should perform this] three times a day.

Having performed worship of the Blessed One, one should offer a bali-oblation. Then, he should strike [the target] with eight thousand *jātī* flowers. This should be accomplished by one who observes the *poṣadha* vows, subsists on a diet of milk and barley-gruel, and sleeps upon a bed of *darbha* grass. He obtains a thousand *dīnāra*s. By constant recitation, he attains success in his journey. If for days...

One should recite [the mantra] seven or eight thousand times; one obtains a village and becomes illustrious. One who desires to produce wealth should go to a cow-pen on the eighth day of the dark fortnight and, subsisting on milk and barley-gruel, recite it one hundred thousand times. On the fourteenth day of the following dark fortnight, having fasted for a day and night, one should recite it one hundred thousand times at that very same place.
One obtains eight hundred *dīnāras*. Whatever one desires—be it gold or a village—one obtains it.

Having fasted for a day and night on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should kindle a fire before the cloth painting (*paṭa*) with wood from the Bodhi tree and recite the mantra eight thousand times over *vacā* root; one will obtain a hundred *dīnāras*. [On] the eighth day of the dark fortnight...
Having kindled a fire with *palāśa* wood, one should offer one hundred thousand pellets of *guggulu* resin smeared with curd, honey, and clarified butter before the cloth painting.

One obtains one hundred dīnāras. One should offer a hundred thousand *śatapuṣpa* flowers; one obtains one hundred dīnāras. One should offer one hundred thousand *bilva* fuel-sticks; one accomplishes whatever one desires. On the bank of the Gaṅgā river or on a seashore, in a place that is uninhabited by humans and undisturbed, [one should fashion] in the sand an image measuring one span of the Sugata.
Having constructed a stūpa according to one’s means and having offered perfumes, flowers, and incense, one should perform the consecration eight thousand times with mantras.
Thus, by offering perfumes and so forth day after day until one thousand and eight stūpas are completed, one attains the binding of the turban.
One should offer eight thousand sesame seeds into the fire; whoever desires this comes under one's control.
Having performed worship at a *caitya* containing relics, one should recite [the mantra] eight thousand times; it will then declare what is auspicious and inauspicious.

One who wishes to perform an empowerment (*āpyāyana*) should offer eight thousand oblations of fuel-sticks from a milk-tree smeared with ghee before the Blessed One. Thereupon, that *vidyā* becomes empowered. On the seventh [day],...

It should be employed in the ritual practice (*sādhana*). Having gone to a place where a *brahmarākṣasa* or another being has completed the preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*), one should recite [the mantra] ten thousand times; it will bestow a great treasure. Subsisting on milk and barley-gruel, one should recite for one year at a shrine containing relics (*sadhātuka-caitya*). Having installed the painted cloth (*paṭa*) in that very place, one should fast for three nights on the eighth day of the dark fortnight.

Having performed a grand worship and offered a sacrificial oblation (bali) before the cloth painting, one should kindle a fire and offer eight thousand oblations of fuel-sticks from the *vaṭa* tree smeared with curd, honey, and ghee. The yakṣas, headed by Kubera, will arrive; one must not be afraid. Having established [the deity] there, one should sit upon a well-formed cushion in the cross-legged posture (*paryaṅka*).

Having firmly grasped it with the hand, one should recite [the mantra] until it blazes. During this interval, it pacifies the suffering of all those in the hells and the animal realm. The assemblies of vidyādharas gather together.
Then, having paid homage to all the buddhas and bodhisattvas, it should be taken up.
Followed by Vidyādharas, he goes to the city of the Vidyādharas; he becomes a king of the Vidyādharas;

all the Vidyādharas worship him; he remains for a great aeon (mahākalpa). By this procedure, specific weapons such as the discus, sword, and mallet are to be accomplished. If this vidyā is being accomplished...

It is not accomplished by this alone; rather, having performed worship before the Blessed Buddha and the painting while reciting this mantra eight thousand times, one should sleep there upon a bed of *kuśa* grass. Whatever one seeks—whether deficient or in excess—in that place, there is the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) accompanied by *yakṣas* and *yakṣiṇīs*. There, one should smear a mandala.
One should offer eight thousand oblations of white mustard seeds. She arrives; she may be addressed as one desires.

When requested, she bestows [her power]; by consuming her, one attains a lifespan of a kalpa. If she does not come, one should perform the rite for seven nights; then she arrives. Now, if one wishes to perform a rite of pacification, [one should do so] before the Blessed One.
One should offer eight thousand oblations of milk, or sprinkle with scented water;
peace will ensue. Or, one should wipe away the bite of a snake with a stalk of *pallagha* grass or a peacock’s eye-feather; it becomes free of poison.
Having ascended the summit of an anthill, fasting and standing on one foot, one should recite [the mantra] from the forenoon until the afternoon.
Whatever is to be experienced through karma (*niyatavedanīya*) is exhausted. That place where one stands is the site for the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*).
Having gone there, having smeared a mandala, one should offer eight thousand oblations of white mustard seeds. Then the yakṣas arrive.
An *arghya* offering should be given with the vessel of scented water that was previously set out. The *yakṣas* will ask, "What must be done?

[The practitioner] should say, "We have been summoned. He should say, "O *yakṣas*, you must become executors of my commands. Having said, "So be it," the *yakṣas* vanish. They become accomplished; whatever one seeks, they give it. It is divine.

They provide elixirs of taste and medicinal prescriptions. Then, even for one surrounded by a thousand followers, they provide food of the six flavors. Whatever one seeks, all that they provide. Thus, for the purpose of subjugation, having fasted for three nights before either of the two black [deities], and having performed protection and being well-restrained, one stands before the cloth painting.

One should offer eight thousand oblations of guggulu resin pills smeared with clarified butter into smokeless embers. At midnight, the deity arrives and should be addressed. She bestows medicinal herbs or whatever one seeks.
One who desires clothing should offer eight thousand oblations of dūrvā grass stalks smeared with clarified butter; he obtains garments.

Having consecrated *vacā* root eight thousand times with mantras and placing it in one's mouth, one becomes the superior disputant in all legal proceedings. Having recited [mantras] over fragrant oil, one should anoint the face; one will become the superior disputant in royal courts.
Having consecrated collyrium eight thousand times with mantras, one should apply it to the eyes; one will become the superior disputant in legal proceedings.
During an eclipse of the moon or sun, one should place *śrotāñjana* in the mouth and recite the mantra as long as the eclipse lasts until it is released.
Having ground it and performed the protection rite, one should consecrate the collyrium eight thousand times with the mantra and apply it to the eyes;
one becomes invisible. One should offer a hundred thousand oblations of all types of perfumes before the cloth painting (*paṭa*); one beholds Śrī. Whomever...
One seeks a boon; one obtains it. Remaining silent and subsisting on alms, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times; one becomes invisible.

Having smeared a mandala in front of the cloth painting and scattered flowers upon it, one should drink seven handfuls of water consecrated with the mantra for seven days; one becomes wise and does not forget what was previously studied.
It is destroyed. One should drink one *karṣa* of the juice of *brahmī* and one *karṣa* of milk after reciting [the mantra] one hundred and eight times;
day by day, one's intelligence increases. For twenty-one nights, one retains and grasps five hundred [verses].
For protection, water consecrated seven times should be applied to the head. This constitutes the binding of the mandala.

One causes possession by means of twenty-one *khadira* wood pegs over which [the mantra] has been recited twenty-one times, or by means of *guggulu* incense. Treatment for poison is performed with a small knife, or the destruction of planetary afflictions (*graha*) is achieved with a sprout.

One should bathe those possessed by planetary spirits with white flowers or guggulu incense over which the mantra has been recited seven times. A thread should be tied [around the patient]. One should offer as an oblation white mustard seeds mixed with sesame seeds and anointed with ghee; he will become a granter of boons. The oblation should be performed at night. On the full moon day, at a stūpa containing relics, one should respectfully smear a mandala and [offer] eight...

One should recite the mantra while burning flowers, garlands, agallochum, turuṣka, sandalwood, and kunduru incense, with eight full jars present. Then, it bestows the accomplishment of the body. At a reliquary containing relics, subsisting on milk and barley gruel, one should perform worship according to one's means and recite the mantra one hundred thousand times for rites such as paralyzing and deluding.
One becomes capable. Eating only barley meal (*saktu*), one should descend into a river up to one's shoulders and recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times.

In the practice of subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*), one becomes highly proficient in applications such as invisibility (*antardhāna*) and the use of stones and other materials. One should offer oblations of cotton seeds (*karpāsāsthi*) at a serpent (*nāga*) shrine; the serpents will become submissive, and whatever one seeks, that one obtains.
Having consecrated the fingers of the right hand eight times with the mantra, one should threaten the king; he will become submissive.

By this very same procedure, one can paralyze elephants, tigers, buffaloes, and the like. Through an oblation of sesame seeds, there is the subjugation of men and women. Through the sale of [consecrated] grain, there is protection—protection for oneself and protection for others. With seven consecrations, there is the binding of the topknot (*śikhābandha*). In battle...

In a dispute within a royal court, victory comes to one who recites this mantra. If one desires to perform a consecration for oneself, one should take four jars filled with water from a river, a pond, or a spring that is not in its season, cast all types of fragrant seeds into them, empower them with eight thousand recitations, and then consecrate oneself with that water.

One becomes liberated from all obstacles, Vināyakas, and Alakṣmī. In the case of a Piśāca fever, one should sprinkle [the patient] with scented water over which the mantra has been recited eight hundred times; he becomes restored to health. For a Vetāḍa, having properly consecrated stakes of Khadira wood and Vālāśallaka with the mantra, one should drive them into the ground facing east.

Having stationed men with swords in their hands in the four directions with great effort, one should sit upon the heart of the Vetāḍa and offer iron filings with an iron ladle (*sruva*). From its mouth, a tongue emerges;
having cut it off with a sharp weapon, it becomes a sword resembling a blue lotus. When that [sword] is grasped, [one attains power].

Accompanied by his retinue, he flies up and becomes a king of the *vidyādharas*. He lives for eleven hundred million years, and when his time has come, he is reborn among the gods. Having fashioned a *muṇḍi* made of "flower-metal" (*puṣpaloha*) endowed with the auspicious marks, one who has performed the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*) should consecrate it for seven nights before the cloth painting and offer a thousand oblations of *sampāta*.

On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, having fasted for three nights in the presence of the Blessed One, having performed a magnificent worship, having carried out the offering of oblations (*balividhāna*), the binding of the boundary of the protection circle (*rakṣāmaṇḍalasīmāvandha*), and so forth, and having fed the noble Saṅgha according to his ability, he should prostrate at their feet, seek permission from the noble Saṅgha, and then die.
Having placed a heap of white mustard seeds at the edge of a cloth painting (*paṭa*), one should recite the mantra over the heap and then offer it;
this effects the expulsion of all planetary seizures (*graha*). By means of guggulu incense, there is the pacification of all untimely death (*akālamṛtyu*).

The stilling of all winds and clouds: having recited the mantra over mustard seeds, one should cast them forcefully into the sky; this is the stilling of all clouds. A stake of *khadira* wood, consecrated seven times with the mantra, should be driven [into the ground]; one becomes free from poison. In all cases of strife, quarrel, conflict, and dispute, a five-colored thread should be empowered one hundred and eight times with the mantra.
Having prepared it, it should be worn on a secret part of the body; all feuds, quarrels, conflicts, and disputes will be paralyzed.

For all regions, water consecrated seven times with mantras should be given; one becomes free from poison. One who desires wealth, being pure and dressed in clean garments, having fasted for a day and night, should offer *kunduruka* incense before the cloth painting (*paṭa*).

In a dream, he reveals what is auspicious or inauspicious. One obtains seven thousand *rūpakas*. For the sake of enjoyment, one who desires wealth should smear all the seals with ashes, establish the cloth-painting (*paṭa*) at the confluence of rivers, or in one of the ponds, or in another pure location, and commence the recitation (*jāpa*) and fire-offering (*homa*). [The offering should consist] of lotuses smeared with curd, honey, and ghee.
One should offer one hundred thousand oblations, or two hundred thousand. Thereupon, one attains all desires. By offering three hundred thousand oblations, one bestows a kingdom.

By offering twenty-one oblations, one becomes a great lord of wealth. One should offer eight thousand pills of guggulu resin smeared with curd, honey, and ghee for twenty-one nights. Prosperity ensues.

One obtains a thousand *dīnāras*. It should be thrown against a wall; all enemies will become paralyzed. Having made a circle of cow dung, having taken a thread and placed it in the middle of the circle, and having offered *guggulu* incense, one should recite the mantra. If [the person] is alive, the thread dances; if not alive, it does not dance. [This is done] with cow dung.

Having smeared a mandala measuring four cubits in size and offered flowers and incense, one should remain standing upon it and recite the mantra. This effects the immobilization of enemies. Having consecrated a weapon seven times with the mantra, it should be buried in the ground; all hostile armies will be cut off. [One should likewise consecrate] the army of an enemy host seven times...

Having recited [the mantra], it should be deposited; one becomes invulnerable. It is a destroyer of epilepsy. Having kindled a fire with *apāmārga* fuel-sticks, one should offer oblations of black sesame seeds mixed with white *karavīra* flowers; the seizing spirits of epilepsy are destroyed.
In all fevers, a black thread should be tied on; for all seizing spirits and *ḍākinīs*, a blue thread [should be tied].
It should be bound. When there is the appearance of portents, such as boils, pustules, sores, or copper-colored discolorations, it becomes white clay and ash.

During an eclipse of the moon or sun, all sentient beings should observe a fast and recite the mantra over oil. They should then smear their faces with that oil and enter the enemy's camp; a mind of loving-kindness will arise [in them]. By this very procedure, one should perform the *pratisaraṇa* (protection).
Having consecrated [it] with the *kṣā* mantra and bound it on the hand, one may enter into battle; one becomes unconquered. Rising at dawn, [one should do so] before a reliquary (*sadhātuka*).

Having made a *gomaya*-maṇḍala at a shrine (*caitya*), one should drink two handfuls of water after reciting [the mantra] seven times over each one; it should be drunk without speaking. At the time of the morning meal, one should eat after first reciting the mantra three times over the initial conversation. In the evening, one should go to sleep after reciting it one hundred and eight times. [This applies to] all rites.

One becomes purified; there is purity of speech. Day by day, one memorizes a hundred verses. Thus, for seven days, having consecrated water seven times with the recitation [of the mantra], one then achieves mastery over the fingers. Then, by means of the finger, one draws [objects] toward oneself. Whomever one touches becomes submissive. Having consecrated clay with the recitation, it should be applied as a binding; it becomes severed.

If one is bound, one should recite [the mantra] seven times over the hand and wipe it upon a stomachache; one becomes healthy. Having recited it three times over the corner of the robe, the corner of the robe should be tied; thieves become bound. Having recited it over oil, it should be applied to the body; whatever one gives, that one receives. Having made a mandala of cow dung...
Having filled an iron vessel with ashes that has been strewn with flowers, one should place it in the center of the mandala.

After reciting the mantra over a cotton wick eight hundred times, one should stand upon it. Having offered incense of guggulu while reciting the mantra, one should snap the fingers. Wherever the thief goes, having made a small circle with the ashes, he...

One becomes subject [to control]. For the immobilization (*stambhana*) of all beings, one should visualize them and, on the day of the full moon during the bright fortnight, kindle a fire before the painting with wood from a Bodhi tree and offer eight thousand sesame seeds as an oblation;
[the beings] will become subject. Having consecrated a stake of *khadira* wood one hundred and eight times, one should bury it in the four directions.

The binding of the boundary is accomplished; the binding of the mandala is accomplished. By water consecrated twenty-one times, there is the expulsion of sentient beings. One should recite over mustard seeds in front of an angry person, and he becomes pacified. Now, if one desires to bring a king under control, [one should offer] fuel-sticks of *arka* wood smeared with curd, honey, and ghee in front of the cloth painting (*paṭa*).

One should offer ten thousand oblations; [the target] becomes submissive. This is the ritual for subjugating a finger. Having offered perfumes, flowers, and incense before the cloth painting (*paṭa*), one should place the right index finger upon seven *aśvattha* leaves and recite the mantra ten thousand times. One receives gold coins and garments for oneself and gives them to a third person.

One should offer eight thousand oblations of clarified butter; one becomes wise. One should offer eight thousand oblations of *nāgakesara* flowers; one obtains a maiden. One should offer eight thousand oblations of *jātī* flowers; one obtains garments.
By reciting [the mantra] one hundred thousand times, one becomes a rememberer of past lives (*jātismara*). There are seven hundred types of diseases; [by this practice], one hundred thousand [times].

Subsisting on milk and barley-gruel, one performs the preliminary ritual (*puraścaraṇa*). Having fasted for three nights on the eighth day of the bright fortnight, and having performed a grand worship of the cloth-painting (*paṭa*), one should recite [the mantra] until a ray of light issues forth. Then one becomes accomplished (*siddha*).
One obtains whatever one contemplates in the mind—whether sovereignty or the state of a *vidyādhara*. Merely by the recitation [of the mantra], it is achieved.
All evil friends are paralyzed;

all obstacles and Vināyakas are destroyed. Having wrapped [the object] with a red thread, it should be placed within a pair of earthenware bowls in a reliquary containing sacred relics (*sadhātuka-caitya*).

Having performed worship before the image, one should recite [the mantra] until the threefold accomplishment occurs. When it becomes warm, one can travel five hundred *yojanas* on foot; furthermore, all those who travel on foot become subject to one's will. When it emits smoke, there is invisibility; [one can walk] four finger-breadths above the ground.

One should not touch it. One lives for a thousand years; one travels a thousand *yojanas*; one possesses the strength of ten men. When [the fire] blazes, one lives for three *kalpas*; one becomes a *vidyādhara* and becomes invincible.
On every full moon of the fifteenth day, being observant of the *poṣadha* vow, in front of the cloth painting, [one should offer] oblations of curd, honey, and ghee...

One should offer ten thousand lotuses as oblations. Thereupon, a divine woman rises from the fire-pit and grants a boon; she should be accepted either as a mother or as a sister. From that time forward, subsisting on a diet of milk and barley-gruel, one should recite the mantra two hundred thousand times. At the conclusion, having fasted for three nights, one should perform the rite before a reliquary stūpa or an image on the fifteenth day.

Having performed worship before the Blessed One, one should recite the mantra upon a bed of *aśvattha* leaves until a woman of divine form arrives. Having offered her the guest-offering (*argha*), one should request a boon; she bestows food, ornaments, and garments.
One lives for a thousand years. During a lunar eclipse, one should take fresh butter from a cow that has a calf of the same color.

Having fashioned a small image six finger-breadths in length, one who has fasted for four meals, having prepared a bed of *aśvattha* leaves, should recite the mantra eight thousand times and then swallow [the image]. All kings will become submissive.
Taking a pala of *kanakavīcikā* and *manaḥśilā* on the full moon day of the fifteenth, while observing the *poṣadha* vows, one should perform a grand [offering].

Having performed worship with eight thousand fragrant flowers, one should strike [the image] at the heart. For the remainder of the time, one should recite the mantra continuously. One obtains five hundred dīnāras. Having performed worship while observing the *poṣadha* vows, one should recite it one thousand times; it reveals auspicious or inauspicious matters in dreams. One should offer oblations of [substances] smeared with ghee for seven days.

At the three junctions of the day, one should recite the mantra eight thousand times; this brings the king under one's control. Having kindled a fire with wood from the *rājavṛkṣa* tree, one should heat a doll made of *madana* wood—adorned with all ornaments—piercing it with a needle, taking care that it does not melt. By reciting the mantra one hundred and eight times at each of the three junctions, one can summon [beings] even from the underworld (*pātāla*).

Having fashioned a six-finger-long wooden image of Sālabhañjikā out of Aśoka wood, one should take it, ascend a mountain peak, and recite the mantra one hundred thousand times. Subsisting on milk and barley gruel, by reciting it one hundred thousand times, one obtains a village;
by reciting it two hundred thousand times, one performs whatever rites one desires; and by reciting it three hundred thousand times, the veil of karma is removed.

It destroys [obstacles]. By reciting the noble mantra four hundred thousand times, it grants a vision of Śrīdarśana. By reciting it five hundred thousand times, the purification of a Buddha-field occurs. By reciting it six hundred thousand times, one is reborn in whichever world-system one desires.
By reciting it seven hundred thousand times, one attains a dhāraṇī. One who wishes to paralyze fire [should do so as follows].

Having recited [the mantra] seven times over a strip of cloth, it should be placed in the mouth. The same success is achieved with water. In a dispute, having consecrated a thread one hundred and eight times, three knots should be made; one will become the respondent.

On the fifteenth day, having placed a *pala* of cow’s ghee in a vessel before the noble Mañjuśrī, and having offered a *gomaya*-maṇḍala and incense of *agaru*, one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times and then drink it. Having drunk it, one must not sleep;
one becomes wise. For seven days, this [rite] effects the expulsion of fevers and the expulsion of *bhūtas*.

Self-protection, the raising of a *vetāḍa*, entry into a cave, entry into a forest, protection, the binding of boundaries, and the binding of the directions—by means of recitation (*jāpa*), thieves, tigers, and *ḍākinīs* become paralyzed. One who desires to become invisible should take the root of *śatāvarī*, empower it one thousand times with mantras, and bind it [to oneself]; he becomes invisible. [This is done] before the cloth painting (*paṭa*).

One should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times. Then, having purchased *śatapuṣpā* flowers by means of a "hero's purchase" (*vīrakraya*), one should offer oblations of them smeared with curd, honey, and ghee.

Whatever price they were purchased for, the result becomes a hundredfold that amount. The oblation should be performed for seven days. One should offer eight thousand oblations of *sumanas* fuel-sticks for seven days. Wealth...

One obtains [it]. One should recite [the mantra] for one month before a cloth painting; one obtains four dīnāras. Having consecrated a marīca fruit seven times with the mantra and placed it in the mouth, to whomever one speaks, that person will regard one as a son.
Having performed this before a reliquary containing relics or before an image of the Buddha, one should throw [the fruit] into the water; the fish of the fishermen [will not be caught].

[The following] occur: One should offer eight thousand oblations of *śephālikā* flowers. Incense made from horse dung, over which the mantra has been recited seven times, should be offered; bedbugs will not appear. By means of flowers or fruit over which the mantra has been recited one hundred thousand times, mosquitoes will not appear. This is a method for subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*). At the king’s gate, [one should perform] the chewing of a tooth-stick and the offering of fruit.
The gift of fragrance, binding the earth, binding thieves, paralyzing all fanged beasts, causing paralysis, breaking fetters, stopping water, stopping fire, cleansing poison,
transmuting poison, binding poison, subjugating spirits, and liberation from the seizure of *ḍākinīs*— these are achieved by means of a lost spell using *gorocanā*.

Having written [the mantra] on birch bark, one should recite it one hundred times before the Blessed One at a reliquary stūpa containing relics. At dawn, it becomes perfected. Having recited it seven times over white mustard seeds, one should scatter them in a village or a city;
those who dwell there will sleep as if dead until sunrise. If one desires to bring under control a woman or a man, for whomever...

From whichever side the house faces, one should face that direction and, having recited [the mantra] one thousand times at an improper time (*vikāla*), go to sleep; a vision [of the deity] will be granted. In this manner for seven days, [the target] becomes submissive. By reciting it seven times, there is the binding of the mouths of all fanged creatures. By mental application, there is the binding of medicinal herbs and the binding of hidden treasures.

One should bury twenty-one stakes made of *khadira* wood at the four corners— the locations of the seven treasures— remaining for an eon and being honored by all accomplished adepts (*siddhas*). By this very same rite, the alms-bowl, sword, water-pot, and so forth [are obtained] by a monk during a lunar eclipse.
This should be proclaimed by all these [practitioners]: one who remains in the vow for a kalpa, a celibate student whose gait is unimpeded, wanders at will.

Subsisting on cow-urine and barley-gruel, if one recites the mantra two hundred thousand times, one obtains eight villages. One remains wherever one desires. Having installed the cloth-painting on the shore of the ocean, one should recite it one hundred thousand times; [then] the Sāgara Nāga King [will appear].
One causes [the practitioner] to enter their own abode. One seeks the *cintāmaṇi* jewel; once it is obtained, one becomes a performer of all rites.
One also goes to the buddha-field of the Tathāgata, remaining for an eon, unimpeded.
One should make knots with a thread spun by a maiden that has been consecrated eight thousand times.

All obstacles and impediments are destroyed. One should recite [the mantra] three hundred thousand times while subsisting on alms on a riverbank. Eating sacrificial food (*haviṣya*), one should recite it one hundred thousand times at the confluence of rivers; one becomes invisible and becomes a master of all means of invisibility. Taking a bowl of appropriate measure according to the Vinaya, one should sit cross-legged before the cloth painting (*paṭa*).

Holding a vessel with the right hand, one should recite the mantra until it blazes; then one becomes a *vidyādhara*. Wherever one dwells, there prosperity shall arise. Thus, immeasurable qualities come to be. Now, if one desires to perform a rite of pacification (*śānti*), one should recite eight thousand times over fragrant flowers smeared with curd, honey, and clarified butter.

Supreme peace occurs. This is the rite for nourishment (*pauṣṭika*). Having kindled a fire with fuel-sticks from milk-trees, one should offer eight thousand oblations of sesame, rice, mung beans, black gram, and so forth, along with women, all smeared with curd, honey, and ghee.

Supreme nourishment occurs. Whether with a painted cloth (*paṭa*) or without a cloth, [this should be performed by] one who observes the *poṣadha* vows, has taken refuge in the Three Jewels, and has embraced the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*).

One should recite [the mantra] ten thousand times. Then, on the full moon day or during a lunar eclipse, having offered an oblation (bali) for the fulfillment of all desires, one should fast for a day and night and recite throughout the entire night. Thereafter, one becomes capable of performing all rites;
one becomes unimpeded in all directions; by merely summoning [someone], one restores them to life; and one should send forth water over which the mantra has been recited seven times.
The sick person becomes healthy after drinking [the medicine]. Regarding the flight from planetary spirits (*graha*): by performing a *homa* of mustard seeds one thousand times.

Having installed the cloth-painting (*paṭa*) at the entrance of an asura cave, one who observes the ritual precepts (*niyama*) should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times. An asura maiden will emerge and lead one inside.
Having placed *vaca* in the mouth, one should recite until the threefold accomplishment (*siddhi*) is attained; when it begins to emit heat (*ūṣmāyamāna*), [success is achieved].

Subjugation. By means of [the mantra] while measuring, one achieves invisibility; by means of the blazing [mantra], one travels through the sky. Having consecrated the cloth-painting (*paṭa*) in a reliquary (*caitya*) containing relics, one should begin on the eighth day of the bright fortnight and offer one hundred thousand lotuses; [then] a king will become [subdued].
One who has observed the *poṣadha* vow [should prepare] a [staff] made of red sandalwood, sixteen or twelve finger-breadths in length.
[Regarding] the ritual action... then one should recite [the mantra] three hundred thousand times from the surface of the cloth-painting.
Having performed a magnificent worship on the full moon day, [one should hold] the staff of wood with the right hand...

Holding it with the hand, one should recite [the mantra] until threefold success is attained: when it becomes warm, one becomes the superior debater among all disputants; by its becoming smoky, there is invisibility; by its blazing, there is the power of traveling through the sky. Having completely covered oneself with a white cloth, one should recite until it blazes; then, accompanied by a thousand followers, one flies up.

One should recite [the mantra] before the cloth painting until the threefold accomplishment is attained. Before the cloth painting, one should offer eight thousand oblations of apāmārga wood fuel smeared with curd, honey, and ghee; then a king or a royal minister will become submissive. Subsisting on milk or vegetables, observing the poṣadha vows, one should recite the mantra three hundred thousand times at a shrine containing relics. Then...
On the eighth day of the dark fortnight and on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should offer eight thousand oblations of black sesame seeds;

one will obtain a thousand kārṣāpaṇa coins. One should offer eight thousand oblations of guggulu resin pills before the image; whichever woman or man one desires, that person is brought under one's control. One should offer eight thousand oblations of guggulu resin pills.
Whatever one desires, one becomes beloved by all people and becomes a superior debater in the royal court.

By anointing oneself with [the substance] consecrated eight thousand times, one becomes fortunate. Beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight, standing before the cloth painting, subsisting on milk and barley gruel, bathing three times a day, and changing one's clothes three times a day—

While burning *agaru*, *turuṣka*, and *candana* incense, one should offer the three white foods (*triśukla*). Having offered an outer *bali* for all beings, one should present fragrant flowers—whether aquatic or terrestrial—or fragrant offerings, as well as three lamps of cow-ghee. At the conclusion, having fasted for three nights, a recitation (*japa*) lasting the entire night should be performed for whatever one prays for.

One obtains that [result]. A communal meal (*saṅghabhakta*) should be provided according to one's ability. Having installed the cloth-painting (*paṭa*) in a reliquary (*caitya*) containing relics (*sadhātuka*), and having fasted for three nights, one should offer thirty-two thousand oblations of *ariṣṭa* wood fuel smeared with curd, honey, and ghee. Then, flames will issue from the cloth-painting, and there will be an earthquake and the blazing of lamps.
It issues forth; the garland of flowers moves. By these signs, one becomes accomplished (*siddha*).

Having placed *śrotāñjana* between the leaves of an *aśvattha* tree and offered it into the fire a thousand times, one is freed from great diseases by reciting [the mantra] once for six months. One should recite it for one month; thus, one’s observance (*vrata*) is fulfilled.
By means of guggulu incense, one causes possession in those afflicted by fevers lasting one day, two days, three days, four days, and so forth.

For the purpose of subjugating a woman, one should offer twenty-one oblations of lalāṭā smeared with honey before the cloth-painting (paṭa) at the three junctions of the day for seven nights; they will become subjugated. In the same way, this applies to a widow or a man. [This is done] before the cloth-painting.

One should offer eight thousand oblations of *arka* wood fuel sticks smeared with curd, honey, and ghee; [the target] becomes submissive. One should offer oblations for twenty-one nights at the three junctions of the day for kings, queens, and so forth; then [success] occurs.
Having consecrated one's head three times or seven times at the royal gate, one should enter; one becomes a favorite of the king.

Having consecrated a peacock’s eye (mayūracandraka) one hundred times, one should wipe away poison; it is destroyed. Having placed realgar (manaḥśilā) between the leaves of an *aśvattha* tree, [one should recite the mantra] three hundred thousand times.

One should recite [the mantra]. It removes *gṛdhrasī* (sciatica). For one suffering from fever, one should perform a cleansing with *kuśa* grass and bind a thread spun by a maiden; he will become fortunate. One should offer a hundred thousand *karṇikāra* flowers as a burnt oblation (*homa*); one obtains twelve *koṭis* of garments.
Having fashioned a wheel made of *puṣpaloha* metal and having installed a cloth-painting (*paṭa*) in a reliquary (*caitya*) containing sacred relics...
Having fasted for a day and night and performed a grand worship, one should take up the wheel and recite the mantra until signs appear:
sparks issue forth from the wheel, continuing until it blazes up. Then one becomes accomplished (*siddha*).
All the hosts of *vidyādharas* assemble; together with one's retinue, one flies up [into the air] as a king of the *vidyādharas*, remaining for an eon (*kalpa*).

One whose movement is unimpeded: having risen at dawn, one should recite [the mantra] for one year; he becomes a granter of boons. One should recite twenty-one lakhs in front of the cloth painting (*paṭa*); one becomes a *vidyādhara*. One should recite eleven lakhs; one beholds Noble Mañjuśrī. One should recite seven lakhs in front of the cloth painting; one becomes invisible. One who is afflicted by disease [should recite] in front of the cloth painting...
One should recite [the mantra] twenty-one hundred thousand times; disease will perish. Having performed the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*), one should recite it twelve hundred thousand times;

one will obtain an elixir of mercury (*rasarasāyana*). By consuming that, one becomes free from wrinkles and gray hair. Having recited it two hundred thousand times, one should offer eight thousand oblations of royal mustard seeds; the queen will become submissive.
Within seven nights, she becomes a bestower of wealth upon him, with the exception of matters connected to sensual desire.

One should offer a hundred thousand oblations of *arka* wood fuel before the cloth painting; one obtains a hundred *pala* of gold. One should offer eight thousand parched grains (*lāja*) for seven nights; no obstacles will arise. One should offer eight thousand oblations of oil-cake; one becomes beloved by all people.

It comes to pass: among the three options, one obtains whichever one desires—whether the state of a *vidyādhara*, or a kingdom, or "I become just like the Blessed One. This accomplishment is achieved by one who is compassionate, giving gifts with a mind free from worldly desire (*nirāmiṣa*). Having fasted for a day and night and having performed a grand worship of the cloth painting (*paṭa*), [one attains it].

One should offer eight thousand oblations of *arka* fuel-sticks; whoever one desires will come at that very moment. Having powdered equal parts of agallochum (*agaru*), *priyaṅgu*, and *nāgakesara*, and having placed them in a pair of earthen bowls (*śarāva-sampuṭa*), one should consecrate them eight thousand times before the right image of Maheśvara and [use] it...

Having anointed one’s body, one should offer eight thousand oblations in battle or to a messenger; one becomes invincible and remains undefeated. With eight thousand *nāgapuṣpa* flowers, a king is brought under one’s control. For all diseases—such as scabies, malignant ulcers, or skin eruptions—one should give [the medicine] after consecrating it seven times with mantras.

He recites the mantra for the pacification [of obstacles]. Having performed the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*) and purified his body with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), he should bathe three times a day and perform the recitation (*japa*) one hundred thousand times before the principal image (*mūlapaṭa*).

Thereafter, on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, having performed worship according to one's ability before the cloth painting, one should sit upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass and offer eight thousand oblations of *bilva* wood fuel smeared with curd, honey, and ghee. A ray of light will issue from the head of Noble Mañjuśrī; it shall circumambulate the practitioner...

The image of the Blessed One disappears; thereafter, one beholds Noble Mañjuśrī. If [the practitioner] is to become a universal monarch (*cakravartin*), then the practitioner’s hut blazes with light. By the swaying of a garland of flowers, one becomes a regional king (*māṇḍalika*).
Having made a mandala with white sandalwood before the cloth painting (*paṭa*), and having offered perfumes, incense, flowers, sacrificial food (*bali*), and ointments—

Having given three hundred kesara flowers and taken them, one should light three ghee lamps consecrated eight hundred times, kindle the fire with udumbara wood fuel, and having consecrated each flower eight hundred times, one should offer them into the fire smeared with ghee. Whomever one desires shall be brought under one's control.
Success is achieved within seven nights. For one who recites it three times a day, the five sins of immediate retribution (pañcānantarya) become attenuated.

By reciting it one hundred and eight times every day, even the killing of a Brahmin becomes attenuated. By constant recitation, one obtains whatever village one desires. Whomever one looks upon with the eye, that person comes under one's control. In debate, by means of recitation, one becomes the victor.
One should offer oblations of sesame and black gram to produce wealth. One should offer eight thousand oblations of *vaṭa* tree shoots;

having performed prostrations to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, one should recite [the mantra] ten times, and one will obtain the faculty of hearing. [One should also worship] Noble Mañjuśrī on a cloth painting or a fruit according to the previously mentioned procedure.
It should be painted with colors that do not adhere [to one another]. Having performed worship before it, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times.

Sleeping on a bed of *kuśa* grass, subsisting on milk and barley gruel, bathing three times a day, and dressed in clean garments, one should undertake the eightfold fast (*poṣadha*) and perform the recitation starting from the first lunar day until—

Regarding the "fifteenth": from that [practice], one pacifies disease. Having performed the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*), subsisting on milk, cow urine, or barley gruel (*yāvaka*), bathing three times a day, and observing the *poṣadha* vows, one should install the cloth painting (*paṭa*) in a shrine containing relics (*sadhātuka-caitya*).
Every day, ghee lamps should be lit, and worship should be performed with a thousand lotuses.
The recitation should be performed during the dark fortnight. One should begin the practice on the first day of the bright fortnight.

On the full moon day, having fasted for three nights and performed a grand worship, the all-night recitation should be performed. By the mere act of its blazing, one flies up into the sky and becomes a *vidyādhara*, surrounded by a thousand *vidyādharas*, with the appearance of a sixteen-year-old.
One with curled, ringlet-like hair is to be honored by all the Vidyādharas. Possession [of a person] is achieved through incense;

the destruction of poison through a sprout; and self-protection through recitation (*jāpa*). Beginning on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight and continuing until the fifteenth, one who is pure—[omitted]—and observing the eightfold fast (*aṣṭāṅga-poṣadha*), should seek whatever he desires before the painted cloth (*paṭa*).
One obtains that.
(pdf 155, p.
700) Having consecrated clarified butter one hundred and eight times with the mantra, one should drink it for seven days. One becomes possessed of great intelligence.
One should offer eight thousand *mallikā* flowers before the cloth painting for seven nights; wealth will be produced.

On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight, having fasted for three nights, one should kindle a fire with *udumbara* wood and offer eight thousand *udumbara* fuel-sticks smeared with curd, honey, and ghee. Five...

One obtains hundreds of dīnāras. On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, the Andhra practitioner, observing the poṣadha vow, should light eight thousand lamps and offer eight hundred lamp-wicks as a burnt offering. Thereafter, recitation should be performed; then one regains one's sight. A deaf person, having caused a book to enter the fragrant chamber (gandhakuṭī)...
One should offer eight thousand oblations of lotuses consecrated eight thousand times; peace will ensue.
In front of the cloth painting (*paṭa*), one should offer eight thousand oblations of *mālatī* flowers smeared with curd, honey, and ghee;

peace will ensue. Having performed the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*), on the fifth day of the dark fortnight, [one should place] the cloth painting before a reliquary stūpa (*caitya*) containing relics.
Having established [the deity], performed a great worship, offered a magnificent *bali* oblation, and presented the external *bali* for all elemental spirits (*bhūta*),

one should fashion a small image with *priyaṅgu* powder and draw it. Having performed the binding of the mandala and the binding of the directions, sitting upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass, one should recite the mantra until a meteor falls.
One should recite once more until the cloth trembles; other signs of accomplishment also appear.

Then, having paid homage to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, one flies up and becomes a Vidyādhara. Able to assume any form at will, one hears from a distance of a thousand yojanas and is invulnerable to all Vidyādharas, provided one has performed the preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa).

Having fasted for a day and night on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, having performed a grand worship, and having taken unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) along with clarified butter (*sarpiṣ*), adorned them with perfumes and flowers and fumigated them with incense, one should take them in the right hand and recite the mantra until they burst into flames.
Having placed the *rocanā* (bezoar) before the noble Mañjuśrī in front of the cloth painting (*paṭa*), one should recite the mantra until it bursts into flames. Then...

It should be grasped. By the mere act of grasping it, one becomes possessed of the strength of a nāga; the weapons of others have no power over him. Whomever he commands becomes subject to his will. He lives for three hundred years.
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, having fasted for a full day and night, one should kindle a fire with *bilva* wood in front of the painting.

One should offer eight thousand oblations of fuel-sticks of *vaikaṅkata* wood smeared with pungent oil. For seven days, whichever maiden one desires shall become submissive. On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, having fasted for one night, one should go to a cremation ground, smear a mandala with cow-dung from a cow that has not calved, take an unbroken skull-cup, and wash it with red sandalwood paste.

Having worshipped with red flowers and incense, one should then sit down and attract [the deity] while reciting the mantra until the skull-cup moves; when it moves, success is achieved. Whomever one attracts by means of a finger, that person comes and performs all that is requested.
One who desires to perform a rite of pacification (*śānti*) should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times before the painted image (*paṭa*).
Then the cloth moves, or the image of the Tathāgata moves; the accomplishment of the ritual (*kalpasiddhi*) occurs.
One should make a knot in a blue garment that has been consecrated one hundred and eight times; victory will be achieved for the wrestler.

One should cause ash consecrated twenty-one times to be placed upon the head of a wrestler; victory in battle will ensue. Beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight, one should place [the substance] together with ghee and milk in a copper vessel before a painted image of the deity, recite the mantra one hundred and eight times, and drink it for seven days; one will become a possessor of a retentive memory (*śrutidhara*). This applies if [the practice is performed] before the noble Mañjuśrī.

A ray of light issues from the mudrā; having circumambulated the world-system with its constituent elements (sadhātuka) to the right, it ascends upwards. One becomes a vidyādhara, able to assume any form at will and unimpeded, living for three thousand years.
On the eighth day of the dark fortnight, having fasted for a full day and night and become fearless, one should then [use] that which has been consecrated seven times by the vidyādhara.
The lion must be struck. Then the lion lets out a lion’s roar, and the practitioner becomes motionless.
Within the interval of a *nālikā*, he becomes wise. Then the practitioner should recite the mantra seven times; thereafter, he should mount the lion, and all the *vidyādharas* will assemble.

Accompanied by his retinue, he flies up with a lion as his vehicle; moving with the speed of thought or the wind, surrounded by many Vidyādharas, he remains for an eon. When he dies, he is reborn wherever he desires. This is the Lion Sadhana.
Furthermore, one who wishes to perform the Lion Sadhana again should, on the full moon of the bright fortnight, observe absolute silence and subsist on a diet of milk and barley gruel.

One should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times until the next full moon. Remaining silent and observing the *poṣadha* vows, one should take wood struck by lightning and soak it in milk for seven days. Then, having removed it, one should bathe that wood struck by lightning with white clay mixed with sandalwood water. Thereafter, the practitioner should have a lion fashioned by a goldsmith who observes the *poṣadha* vows.

It should be caused to be made. Then, under the Puṣya constellation, having performed a magnificent worship of the Three Jewels, one should feed the monks designated for the Saṅgha. Having performed a magnificent worship before the cloth painting and offered various sacrificial oblations, the practitioner, being pure and dressed in clean garments, should sit upon a bundle of kuśa grass.
Holding the lion with the right hand, one should recite the mantra until it moves like a lion.
When it moves, various kinds of signs arise. Then, an offering (argha) should be presented. Again, one hundred and eight recitations must be performed.
Mustard seeds will arrive. While reciting the mantra, the lion should be touched; she becomes a woman. She says: "What?"
"I am doing it. She should be told: "She has entered within the body... Then she is bestowed upon the heart of the practitioner.

At that very moment, she becomes eighteen years of age in appearance, with a radiance equal to the rising [sun], possessing the power of a cart and an unimpeded gait. Whomever she looks upon, they... [are subdued]. Thus.
The *vidyādharas* shall become subject to his power. He shall remain for an eon (*kalpa*). When he dies, he is reborn among the gods.
(Having performed the preliminary rites, having installed the cloth painting in a shrine containing relics, [one should recite] five hundred times into the mouth...)

Having installed [the image], one becomes invisible and lives for a thousand years. Having performed the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*), subsisting on a diet of milk and barley-gruel, one should install the cloth-painting (*paṭa*) on a mountain peak, worship it with perfumes, flowers, and incense, and recite the mantra three hundred thousand times. Then, one who observes the ritual fast (*upoṣadha*) should take ashes and earth from an anthill, mix them with milk, and...

Having smoothed it out to the measure of a Sugata-span, a peacock should be painted by a painter observing the *poṣadha* vow using colors that do not adhere [to one another]. Having gone to a secluded place, having set up the cloth painting,
having worshipped it with perfumes, flowers, and incense, and having offered a *bali* sacrifice for all spirits, then, being pure...
Having dressed in clean garments and placed a peacock before the cloth painting, one should recite the mantra until the peacock moves.
Then, the Vidyādhara, holding with his right hand a pair of earthenware bowls (*śarāvasampuṭa*) containing *aparājita* flowers over which the root-mantra has been previously recited,
should recite it until the sound of a jackal’s howl is heard while reciting the mantra.

Having placed living beings into his own mouth for his friends, he becomes invisible; having summoned all the *siddhas*, he lives for two thousand years. Having made a smooth stone with lotus filaments and *sauvīra* collyrium, one should have it ground in the hand of a maiden who has performed the preliminary rites (*pīṣadhikā*). Encased in the three metals, [this should be used] during the conjunction of the Puṣya asterism by one who has completed the preparatory practices (*kṛtapuraścaraṇa*).

Having performed a worship of Maheśvara’s image with a bali offering consisting of all kinds of grains, as well as with perfumes, flowers, and incense, one should place it in a hollowed-out vessel made of two earthen bowls, grasp it with the right hand, and recite the mantra until it makes a rattling sound (*khaṭakhaṭāyati*). Having offered one portion to the Blessed One and distributed the rest among one's companions, [one should then take] *apāmārga* fuel-sticks for oneself...

One should offer ten thousand oblations of items smeared with curd, honey, and ghee; one obtains ten thousand pieces of gold. Taking bamboo-resin (*vaṃśarocanā*), one should fashion pills encased in the three metals;
then, having gone to a cremation ground dressed in pure white garments, one should perform worship with perfumes, flowers, and incense.

Having offered a bali-oblation to all beings and having established a skull-cup filled with *pulikā*, one should recite the mantra until the sound of "kilakila" is heard. One must not be afraid. Having divided it among one's companions and placed it in one's own mouth, one becomes invisible. One lives for ten thousand years. Taking an owl's eye together with collyrium...

Having wrapped it in three metals, one should grind it in the hand of a maiden; then, placing the pill inside a pair of earthen saucers (*śarāva-sampuṭa*), one attracts a *yakṣiṇī* for seven nights before the right-hand image of Maheśvara.
Remaining silent as wood for six months, one should recite [the mantra]; then the substance becomes unspoken [i.e., invisible]. [One should fashion an image] from *rājārka*...

Having fashioned an image six finger-breadths in height and having had it bathed with *aśleṣaka* substances, [the practitioner], remaining silent and adorned [with ornaments], should empower the palm of a *nāga* for six months; having recited the mantra ten thousand times, he obtains a well-hidden treasure.
(From *pdf* 158, p.

703) Having descended to a river flowing to the ocean, one should offer ten thousand oblations of *arka* flowers smeared with curds, honey, and ghee, using an *arka* leaf as the vessel. The Sun becomes a granter of boons. [One should do this] at that very same river...
Having entered water reaching only to the waist, one should offer sesame seeds and flowers; the Grandfather (Brahmā) becomes a granter of boons.

One should offer mandāra flowers; Śakra becomes a granter of boons. In that very water, with mandāra flowers, Dhanada becomes a granter of boons. By reciting the mantra two hundred thousand times, one attracts a king; by reciting it three hundred thousand times—

One attracts all sentient beings. Having descended to a river that flows toward the ocean, one should offer ten thousand *aśoka* flowers. Having performed a grand worship before the original cloth painting (*mūlapaṭa*), and having placed a wheel or a *svastika* upon an *aśvattha* leaf, one should sit in the cross-legged posture and recite the mantra until it blazes. By that—
As soon as it is taken up, one becomes a universal monarch of the Vidyādharas with curly, ringed hair and a complexion like the rising sun;

he flies up together with those who see him and those whom he sees. Having taken the root of the Sudarśana plant, grasped it with the hand, and recited the mantra over it one thousand times, one should bind it to the hand; whoever he touches becomes subject to his will.

Taking a wheel made of *kuśa* grass and reciting [the mantra] one thousand times, one should cast it into water; then a *nāga* rises up and says, "What shall I do? One should say, "Give me a *lakṣa*. Having subsisted on alms-food, one should ascend a mountain peak and recite it one hundred thousand times; the forms of the Tathāgatas will appear before one's eyes. Having seen them, whatever one accomplishes, that [is attained].

Success is attained. Women appear adorned with all ornaments, and men who have propitiated the Buddha attend upon them simultaneously with laughter, dance, and other such delights. Whatever one thinks of, all that comes to pass. At dawn, once it has been removed, everything vanishes. Beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight, one should remain fasting for a day and night before the cloth painting.
Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times over a karṣa of *brahmīsaka*, *karpa*, *gavya*, and ghee, along with a *karṣa* of milk, one should drink it for seven days;

one becomes a possessor of the power of hearing (*śrutidhara*). Having placed a basket of various kinds of food and edibles before the cloth painting, one should recite [the mantra] until the food has vanished; thereafter, the food is transferred [to others].
And [the ritual involves] varieties of rice. Having performed the preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*), one should fashion a sixteen-spoked wheel out of the three metals (*triloha*).

On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, having fasted for a day and night, one should perform worship at a crossroads and sit down. Placing a piece of realgar (*manaḥśilā*) the size of a finger-joint in the mouth, one should recite the mantra until the mouth bursts open. [The result concerns] the realgar.
It becomes accomplished. Having applied a *tilaka*, one becomes invisible, able to assume any form at will, and lives for five hundred years.

On the eighth day of the dark fortnight, having fashioned a small trident from bell-metal (*paṇika*), one should perform the ritual. Having fasted for a day and night, gone to a cremation ground (*śmaśāna*), and performed the worship with the mantras of the trident, one should sit in the cross-legged posture (*paryaṅka*).

Holding a trident with the right hand, one should recite [the mantra] until a ray of light issues forth from the trident; then one becomes accomplished. At night, one should bury it, and a divine house will appear.

It comes to pass. Having established the image in a clean place and fasted for a day and night, one should fashion a small figure before the cloth painting (*paṭa*), worship it according to the ritual rules, and offer eight thousand oblations of *bilva* wood sticks smeared with curd, honey, and ghee.
Then, a ray of light issues from the forehead of the Blessed Mañjuśrī; by that, one becomes accomplished. [The merit is] immeasurable.

One obtains gold as wealth. Having fasted for a day and night, one should take a single *karavīra* flower before the cloth painting, go to a nāga abode, and cast the flower into the nāga pool while reciting the mantra. The nāgas and nāginīs will become submissive; whatever one requests, that one obtains. This applies to one who has completed the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*).

Having fasted for a day and night on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one who desires to destroy fever should offer eight thousand oblations of *girikarṇikā* flowers; the fevers caused by *piśācas* will perish.

By offering one hundred and eight oblations of *khadira* wood fuel-sticks, one causes all seizing spirits (*graha*) to release their hold. [One may also act] with ashes over which the mantra has been recited seven times.

The Lord of Mantras binds the supreme mantras. Liberation occurs by means of water over which the mantra has been recited once. Having written [the mantra] on cloth or birch bark, one should tie it to the top of a banner; the enemy army will then be paralyzed.
Subsisting on water and barley meal, having fasted for three nights on either the eighth or the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should go to a solitary linga and [place it] upon the linga.

Placing the right foot upon the image, one should bind it with *vālaśollaka* grass; having formed a fist, one should recite the mantra until the sound "I am dying" (*marāmi*) emerges. Upon the third such cry, the fist becomes perfected (*siddha*).
Having formed the fist, one lives for seven hundred years and becomes a member of Maheśvara’s retinue. [This is done] with *gorocanā*.
Whomever one sees while applying a forehead mark (*viśeṣaka*) consecrated with a thousand recitations, all become submissive.

Having risen in the morning, having consecrated water seven times and washed one's face, whoever one gives a look to becomes submissive. Likewise, for one desiring food, having consecrated a handful of water seven times with oil...

One should drink [it]. One obtains food without having asked for it. When entering a royal court, one should take a corner of one's robe, recite the mantra over it twenty-one times, and tie a knot with the left hand; thus, one becomes one whose speech is unimpeded.
This should be remembered in the midst of thieves, and it will release even those who are bound. It also heals mantras that are broken, split, or deficient.

Having fashioned an image out of *śāli* rice, *vrīhi* rice, white *karavīra*, and *aryaka* flowers, one should hold it with the left hand before a cloth painting (*paṭa*) and recite the mantra eight thousand times. This constitutes the "raising" (*utthāpana*) of the mantras;
one obtains a thousand cows. By this same method, having burned ghee and resin (*sarjarasa*), one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times.

One obtains twelve excellent villages. Having constructed a stūpa according to this very procedure, one should offer a hundred thousand lotuses smeared with [fragrant substances]. One attains sovereignty over a country. [Having built] a stūpa the size of a *sthī* (a specific measure), while burning [incense], one should offer a hundred thousand *campaka* flowers.
One obtains a thousand gold pieces.
(PDF 160, p.
705) Having constructed a stūpa measuring one span of the Sugata, or having drawn an image of it, one should stand upon it with the left foot.

One should recite [the mantra] eight thousand times; by means of one's lineage, [the person] comes under control. Having constructed a stūpa measuring one span of a Sugata, one should offer eight thousand oblations of wedding parched grains (*lāja*) smeared with curd, honey, and ghee into the fire. With the ashes, one performs the binding of the ritual circle (*maṇḍala-bandha*). Having bathed at dawn, one should churn butter using this very mantra and take hold of it.

Having performed a grand worship and burning incense over which the mantra has been recited eight thousand times, one should consume it without touching it with the teeth; he whose name is used will become submissive. [This applies] except for that which is associated with sensual desire. Having fasted for three nights and performed a grand worship of the cloth painting with all kinds of perfumes purchased from a hero-seller, one should offer a lamp of ghee.

Having kindled [the fire], one should oneself recite the mantra. Having made an effigy with that [substance] and placed it upon seven *aśvattha* leaves, one should recite until it becomes supple. Having reduced that to powder, whoever is touched by it comes under one's control. By this very same procedure, [one may act] with the powder of *nāgakeśara*.

Having fashioned an image, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations of incense in incense-bowls; whoever one contemplates shall be brought under one's control. By this very rite, one desiring wealth should offer oblations of *apāmārga* wood. Having gone to a cow-pen, one should fashion a stūpa one cubit high out of fallen cow-dung in front of the cloth painting (*paṭa*), and worship it according to the prescribed ritual.

While burning guggulu resin, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times. Thus, one becomes invincible to all *vidyādharas* and travels through the seven paths of the wind. Taking the index finger of a child less than a year old and fashioning a stūpa the size of a hand, one should perform worship according to the rules in a cremation ground, seated facing east upon a bed of *kuśa* grass.

Having offered that finger and grasped it with the forefinger, one should recite the mantra until a ray of light issues forth and the flame of the lamp increases. Having performed the protection rites and taken hold of the kingdom, whoever he draws toward himself with that finger at dawn becomes subject to his will. Having fasted for three nights, one should take the milk of a cow that has a calf of the same age and is full of milk, and [place it] before the cloth painting.
Having prepared a mandala and lit a ghee lamp, one should place [the substance] consecrated eight thousand times upon a bed of kuśa grass and prepare milk in an earthen vessel.
A homa for Vināyaka is performed with curd, honey, and ghee. Then, having prepared a mandala, one should place pieces of gold in the four directions.

In the second maṇḍala is Prabodhaka, holding mustard seeds in his hand; in the third maṇḍala is Susahāya. Having performed a great worship, secured protection, and sat facing east, one should grasp [the object] with the hand and recite the mantra until it emits heat, smoke, and bursts into flame. With the first [application], one whose eyes are anointed will see whomever [and whatever].

All see him, and he becomes a master of all [sciences]. By the second [recitation], one possessing the strength of nine thousand nāgas and the speed of the wind lives for five thousand years; he becomes a Vidyādhara who is not surpassed by any, and [the mantra] empowered eight thousand times serves as a means of invisibility.
